title: Multi-omic profiling of 85 iPSC lines from familial dementia reveals cellular diversity and regulators of organoid development.
abstract: Systematic molecular characterization of human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines carrying disease-associated mutations is needed to distinguish disease-related biology from variation in cell state, genomic integrity, and genome-editing history, yet such systematic characterization is uncommon. Here, we profiled 85 human iPSC lines carrying MAPT mutations and isogenic controls using whole-genome sequencing, long-read sequencing of the MAPT locus, bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, and DNA methylation arrays. Single-cell analyses identified four reproducible iPSC states and candidate surface markers for their isolation. Whole-genome sequencing revealed unintended editing events and recurrent 20q11.21 duplications, which were associated with increased ID1 expression and impaired cortical organoid patterning. Transcriptomic analyses identified pathways associated with organoid quality and changes linked to clonal selection and editing, underscoring the need to use unconverted lines as isogenic controls. By providing an in-depth genomic characterization of MAPT iPSCs, this dataset serves as a proof of principle to enhance iPSC utility in biological research.

title: A dataset of differentiable biologically derived single-neuron models.
abstract: Biological neural networks contain diverse cell types with heterogeneous electrophysiological properties. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) model computational aspects of biology but use homogeneous neurons, limiting realism. A key obstacle to building bio-inspired ANNs is the absence of a database of neuron models that both fit biological data and remain differentiable for gradient-based learning. We present such a database: over 1,000 differentiable single-neuron firing-rate models with accompanying PyTorch code. The models belong to the linear-nonlinear (LN) class, which, for ease of reference, we term generalized firing rate (GFR) neurons. Each GFR neuron uses input and firing-rate history filters across multiple timescales, followed by a nonlinearity to generate firing rates. Models are fit to patch-clamp recordings from mouse and human central nervous system slices. Parameter clustering reflects electrophysiological diversity and partially aligns with transgenic lines. This resource will enable development of bio-inspired ANNs built from biologically grounded, differentiable single-neuron models.

title: Predictors of relapse following transition to ofatumumab in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Ofatumumab (OFA) is an emerging therapy for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), but the impact of prior disease-modifying therapy (pDMT) on outcomes after switching is unclear. To evaluate predictors of first-year relapse after switching from selected pDMTs to OFA in adults with RRMS enrolled in the MSBase Registry. Among 866 patients (median EDSS 2.5), 10.5% experienced a relapse in the first year on OFA. Switching from fingolimod was associated with higher relapse risk compared to switching from injectable therapies (HR 1.89, 95% CI 1.03-3.44, p = 0.038). Higher EDSS at OFA initiation (HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.09-1.43, p = 0.001) and relapse in the year prior to pDMT cessation (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.01-3.03, p = 0.045) also predicted relapse. Washout period duration was not associated with relapse in the overall cohort, but longer washout among fingolimod switchers increased relapse risk (HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.01-1.79, p = 0.044). Relapse after switching to OFA is influenced by baseline disability, recent relapse, and prior fingolimod use. Shorter washout may reduce relapse risk in fingolimod switchers. These findings support tailored monitoring and further research to optimise treatment transitions in RRMS.

title: Nanoparticle size-dependent structural observability revealed by surface-enhanced Raman scattering in Alzheimer's disease rat hippocampal tissue.
journal: Spectrochimica acta. Part A, Molecular and biomolecular spectroscopy
abstract: Understanding the structural heterogeneity of protein aggregation in complex biological environments remains a central challenge in biophysical chemistry. Transient and partially ordered aggregation intermediates are particularly difficult to characterize because they exhibit structural diversity, low abundance, and weak spectroscopic signatures. The present within-subject repeated-measures study investigated how gold nanoparticle (AuNP) size influences plasmon-enhanced vibrational spectroscopy used to probe amyloid aggregation in situ. Hippocampal tissue sections from an Alzheimer's disease (AD) rat model were examined using AuNPs of two distinct diameters (20 nm and 80 nm). Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) spectroscopy combined with three-dimensional (3D) Raman imaging was used to investigate nanoparticle aggregation behavior, spectral enhancement, and structural observability within a heterogeneous biological matrix. The present study builds upon our previous observations that Aβ-coated 20 nm AuNPs exhibit nanoparticle-size-dependent quasi-reversible aggregation behavior, suggesting that nanoparticle size influences the structural states accessible during protein assembly. Accordingly, the primary objective of the present work was to clarify how nanoparticle size governs structural observability and molecular selectivity during in situ SERS analysis of amyloid aggregation. The results reveal a pronounced nanoparticle-size dependence in the SERS response. Smaller nanoparticles preferentially enhance vibrational features associated with dynamic and weakly ordered protein conformations characteristic of aggregation intermediates. The preferential observation of several localized vibrational modes in the 20 nm AuNP datasets further indicates that the reduced spectral occupancy should not be interpreted as reduced analytical sensitivity. Rather, it implies selective access to conformationally diverse and dynamically evolving molecular environments that are not strongly represented in the 80 nm datasets, consistent with previously reported nanoparticle-size-dependent quasi-reversible aggregation behavior. In contrast, 80 nm nanoparticles preferentially enhance vibrational features associated with more extended and highly ordered aggregate structures. Three-dimensional Raman imaging further demonstrated that these distinct structural states are associated with markedly different aggregate architectures and spatial extents within hippocampal tissue from the AD rat model, consistent with nanoparticle-size-dependent structural observability. These findings establish nanoparticle size as a key physical parameter governing plasmon-molecule coupling and structural observability in SERS. The use of multiple nanoparticle sizes therefore provides a practical strategy for resolving weakly ordered aggregation-associated states in situ and establishes a spectroscopic framework for investigating protein assembly pathways in complex biological environments.

title: Fear-antagonistic actions and safety behaviors in the treatment of acrophobia: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Exposure therapy effectively treats anxiety disorders, yet non-response and premature dropout motivate continued work on procedural enhancements. Fear-antagonistic actions, behaviors that directly oppose fear-driven action tendencies (e.g., walking briskly toward and leaning over a railing rather than standing back from the edge), can augment exposure, but performing them necessarily precludes safety behaviors. This study examined whether fear-antagonistic actions confer augmentation effects beyond safety behavior elimination alone. University students and community adults with long-standing, clinically significant fear of heights (N = 109; 68% female; mean age = 21.8 years) were randomly assigned to standard exposure (EXP; n = 32), exposure with safety behavior fading (EXP+SBF; n = 31), exposure with safety behavior fading plus fear-antagonistic actions (EXP+SBF+AA; n = 35), or waitlist control (WLC; n = 11). Peak fear during a behavioral approach test in a novel (generalization) context served as the pre-designated primary outcome. Both EXP + SBF + AA and EXP + SBF outperformed EXP on peak fear in the treatment and generalization contexts through 1-month follow-up, and all active conditions outperformed WLC. EXP + SBF + AA and EXP + SBF did not significantly differ on any primary or secondary outcome (all ps > .140). Bayes factors provided moderate evidence against differential change on the primary outcome (BF01 = 6.1), although equivalence tests could not exclude small-to-moderate differences. Marked reductions in height overestimation occurred for all active groups and were sustained at 1-month follow-up. Findings indicate that safety behavior elimination is the robust active ingredient driving augmentation effects; any incremental benefit of fear-antagonistic actions is likely small.

title: Estimating the eligible population for amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibody therapy in memory clinics: Application to lecanemab in France.
journal: The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Lecanemab was the first amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibody approved by the European Commission for treating patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease (AD). While this marketing authorization led to heterogeneous situations across European countries, France declined reimbursement, citing limited clinical benefit and concerns about the healthcare system's capacity to implement this new care pathway. This capacity depends directly on the number of eligible patients, yet robust estimates remain limited and highly variable across studies. Our objective was therefore to estimate the population eligible for lecanemab in France. Using transportability methods based on inverse odds of selection weighting, we articulated the nationwide consultation data from the French National Alzheimer Database (BNA) with the deeply phenotyped MEMENTO clinical cohort. Eligibility for lecanemab followed the French appropriate use recommendations: 1) clinical eligibility (age 50-90 years, MCI with common AD phenotype or mild AD dementia, MMSE ≥22), 2) biological eligibility (amyloid confirmation determined sequentially using plasma p-tau217, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers and amyloid-PET), 3) absence of contraindications (APOEε4 homozygosity, anticoagulant use, MRI risk markers for ARIA). Among patients consulting French memory clinics, 19.5% met clinical eligibility criteria. Of these, 73.0% (95%CI: 67.6-77.9) were amyloid-positive, and 49.7% (95%CI: 44.0-55.5) remained eligible after applying safety criteria. Overall, 9.7% (95%CI: 8.6-10.8) of patients consulting memory clinics were estimated to be eligible for lecanemab, representing approximately 18,200 individuals nationally (annual average, 2022-2024). These results inform healthcare planning for disease-modifying therapy implementation in France and comparable countries.

title: CNPY3 variants associated with a recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy affect inflammasome and TLR function.
abstract: Canopy FGF signalling regulator 3 (CNPY3) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident chaperone essential for toll-like receptor (TLR) folding, trafficking and inflammasome activation. In rare paediatric cases, biallelic CNPY3 variants have been associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), but available data remain sparse. 50 individuals from 38 unrelated families with biallelic CNPY3 variants and DEE were evaluated for exome and genome findings, standardised clinical phenotype descriptions, EEG results, and neuroimaging data. A selection of variants underwent functional analysis focussing on protein stability and localisation, TLR2 function, NLPR3 inflammasome activation, and structural conformation. Disease onset occurred in early infancy (median age at onset 68 days), with a clinical phenotype comprising global developmental delay (100%) and intractable epilepsy (86%), accompanied by microcephaly (70%), spasticity (77%), growth faltering (63%), stridor (48%), and early mortality (38%). Epileptic spasms and tonic seizures (46% each) were the most frequent seizure types, and EEG findings included suppression-burst (37%) and hypsarrhythmia (28%). Phenotypic severity varied substantially, with most patients being severely affected (median score 16, range 2-20). Most variants occurred in the homozygous state (95%), including 13 missense changes and 7 truncating alleles. Variants were classified as of uncertain significance (71%), followed by likely pathogenic (23%) and pathogenic (6%) according to ACMG/AMP criteria. Genotype-phenotype correlation showed that individuals with truncating variants were, on average, more severely affected than those with non-truncating variants (median score 18 vs 14.5). Protein modelling predicted conformational effects for most missense variants. In cells, frameshift alleles abolished CNPY3 protein expression, whereas nonsense alleles markedly reduced protein levels. ER localisation of CNPY3 remained preserved across tested genotypes; however, capacity to support TLR2 maturation and processing varied substantially. Remarkably, some missense variants permitted TLR2 surface expression but impaired downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, uncoupling trafficking from signal transduction. CNPY3-associated DEE is a severe early-onset disorder with genotype-dependent phenotypic severity, accompanied by allele-specific disruption of innate immune pathways. Our findings reveal separable effects on TLR trafficking, downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, identifying CNPY3 as a key regulator of multiple cellular pathways involved in inflammatory responses and neurodevelopment. title: Lateral habenula hyperactivity and network dysfunction underpin stress-induced depressive-like behaviors in mice.
abstract: The lateral habenula (LHb) is a critical hub for encoding aversive signals and regulating negative motivation in depression, yet the systemic alterations in functional connectivity and topological architecture of LHb-centered whole-brain networks induced by chronic stress remain unclear. This study characterized LHb-associated network changes in chronic social defeat stress (CSDS)-induced depressive-like male mice using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, including fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF), static/dynamic functional connectivity (sFC/dFC) and graph theory analysis, combined with a battery of behavioral assessments. CSDS-susceptible mice exhibited typical depressive phenotypes (social avoidance, anhedonia, behavioral despair), accompanied by elevated spontaneous neuronal activity in the LHb, robust hyperconnectivity between the LHb and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, and significantly reduced dFC variability between the LHb and subcortical regions (hippocampus, hypothalamus, midbrain). Graph theory analysis further revealed a disrupted small-world topology of the LHb-centered network, with decreased global/local efficiency, reduced clustering coefficient and increased characteristic path length. Our findings reveal that chronic stress exposure is associated with LHb hyperactivity and widespread fronto-limbic and subcortical network remodeling. The functional and topological LHb signatures identified herein may serve as candidate biomarkers indicating stress susceptibility. This study offers multi-layered interpretative clues for network-level alterations linked to stress-associated depressive manifestations, and identifies the LHb connectome as a promising circuit candidate for follow-up targeted interventional research of mood disorders.

title: Antinociceptive interaction of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol in a humanized mouse model of sickle cell disease.
journal: The Journal of pharmacology and experimental therapeutics
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is characterized by recurrent, debilitating pain. Opioid analgesics are routinely used in its management, but limited efficacy and pervasive side effects prompt many patients with SCD to seek alternatives, including cannabis. Prior work has shown that 2 major cannabis constituents, Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC) and cannabidiol (CBD), exert antinociceptive effects in HbSS-BERK mice, a model of SCD. The present study investigated the pharmacological interaction between these 2 agents and characterized the effects associated with repeated coadministration. Fixed-ratio isobolographic analyses demonstrated that Δ9-THC and CBD produced dose-dependent antinociception following acute coadministration. Fixed-ratio isobolographic analyses showed that the experimentally determined median effective dose of the mixture was lower than the theoretical additive dose, but the difference was not statistically significant, supporting an additive antinociceptive interaction. Repeated coadministration maintained antinociceptive efficacy over 14 days and reduced SCD-evoked anxiety-like behavior in one cohort but did not improve recognition-memory deficits. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry analyses revealed that repeated coadministration increased plasma CBD concentrations, produced a modest increase in Δ9-THC exposure, and markedly elevated circulating levels of the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoyl-sn-glycerol. Molecular analyses of spinal cord tissue showed that HbSS-BERK mice exhibited increased oxidative stress (malondialdehyde, MDA) and proinflammatory signaling (interleukin [IL]-1β mRNA), with no change in anti-inflammatory signaling (IL-10 mRNA). Following 14 days of treatment, CBD reduced MDA and IL-1β transcription, whereas Δ9-THC reduced MDA and increased IL-10. Notably, the combination treatment simultaneously reduced oxidative stress, suppressed IL-1β, and enhanced IL-10. Together, these findings demonstrate an additive antinociceptive interaction between Δ9-THC and CBD and sustained efficacy during repeated administration in SCD mice. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Chronic pain in sickle cell disease remains difficult to treat, and many patients use cannabis despite limited understanding of how its constituents interact to produce analgesia. This study demonstrates that the 2 major phytocannabinoids in cannabis, Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol, produce additive antinociceptive effects in a humanized mouse model of sickle cell disease, and their combined efficacy is maintained during repeated administration without detectable tolerance.

title: Corrigendum to "LPI alleviates Alzheimer's disease pathology via the GPR55 receptor" [Neuroscience 611 (2026) 99-110].
Electric field strength, hippocampal volume change, and cognitive outcomes following electroconvulsive therapy: the role of sex and anatomy.
abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) induces hippocampal volume alterations, but the clinical significance of the volumetric change remains unclear. Greater electric field (EF) strength has been associated with increases in hippocampal volume and decline in cognitive performance following ECT, and this association might be moderated by individual-level variables, such as sex. In this study, 29 patients with severe or treatment-resistant depression underwent right unilateral ECT. EF strength was simulated using ROAST, and hippocampal volumes were segmented with FreeSurfer. Cognitive performance was assessed pre- and post-ECT using a multidomain neuropsychological battery. Associations between EF strength, hippocampal volume change, and cognitive outcomes were analyzed, with sex as a moderator. At the group level, ECT reduced depressive symptom severity, without cognitive decline. Female patients exhibited higher EF strength in bilateral hippocampi, associated with smaller intracranial volumes and greater changes in the left hippocampal volume following ECT. Exploratory analyses indicated that higher EF strength and greater left hippocampal volume increase were linked to smaller improvement in verbal memory performance; moreover, a sex×volume interaction suggested opposite trends by sex, with volume increase correlating with greater improvement in males but smaller in females. Greater hippocampal volume change was also linked to lower consistency in autobiographical memory; however, post-hoc sensitivity analysis indicated that this association was outlier-driven and should be interpreted with caution. Our findings suggest that individual anatomical variability influences the EF and may contribute to cognitive side effects following ECT. Awareness of anatomy-related EF differences may inform future research strategies for individualized treatment planning and cognitive monitoring.

title: Generation of a CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic control iPSC line (NIMHi001-A-1) from a Parkinson's disease Patient-Derived iPSC line carrying the LRRK2 I1371V mutation.
abstract: We report NIMHi001-A-1, a CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic iPSC line derived from a patient line carrying a heterozygous LRRK2 missense mutation GRCh38 chr12:g.40308618A > G [(MANE transcript NM_198578.4:c.4111A > G); p.Ile1371Val] associated with familial Parkinson's disease. Sanger sequencing confirmed successful correction. The line retained iPSC morphology and expressed pluripotency markers (OCT4, NANOG, SOX2, TRA-1-60, SSEA4) by immunofluorescence, gene expression analysis, and flow cytometry. Normal karyotype (46, XY) and complete genetic identity with the parental line were established by STR profiling. No off-target modifications were detected. The line demonstrated trilineage differentiation potential and tested negative for mycoplasma, providing an isogenic platform to investigate LRRK2 I1371V-specific pathomechanisms and evaluate therapeutic strategies.

title: Finding the right words in connected speech: An examination of word-finding difficulties in persons with multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Self-reported word-finding difficulties are common in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS). A lack of suitable methods for assessing these sometimes-subtle word-finding difficulties in PwMS has been highlighted. The aim of this study was to investigate how word-finding difficulties can be detected and how they manifest themselves in connected speech in PwMS compared to non-brain-damaged (NBD) controls. Twenty-seven PwMS with self-reported anomia and 23 NBD controls performed a video-retelling task which was evaluated by (i) counting the number and types of indicators of word-finding difficulties, (ii) main-concept analysis (MCA), and (iii) correct-information-unit (CIU) analysis. Additionally, correlations between word-finding ability in connected speech, picture-naming ability, verbal fluency and demographic and disease-related factors were explored. Content analysis of connected speech proved to be successful in confirming self-perceived difficulties. In line with their own perceptions, word-finding difficulties were significantly more frequent in the MS group than in the NBD group (U = 144, p < .001). The overall distribution of WFD types differed significantly between groups, χ²(13) = 76.21, p < .001. In particular, the MS group had significantly more pauses and lower speech rate (U = 89, p < .001). In the MS group, a high frequency of indicators of word-finding difficulties was related to low MCA and CIU scores and to a low score on a phonemic verbal-fluency test, but no correlations were found between word-finding difficulties on the one hand and age, years of education, or disease-related factors such as MS type, disease duration, or Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score on the other.

title: A multi‑target adverse outcome pathway network for sub-chronic ketamine‑induced cognitive impairment in adult zebrafish.
abstract: Ketamine (KET), an emerging contaminant, is increasingly detected in aquatic environments, yet its sub-chronic neurocognitive effects at environmentally relevant concentrations remain largely unknown. We exposed adult zebrafish to KET for 40 days and integrated network toxicology, transcriptomics, behavioral assays, and molecular simulations to investigate these effects. Sub-chronic KET exposure impaired spatial learning and memory at 0.4 μg/L, while anxiety‑like and social behavior were altered only at 40 μg/L. Intersecting transcriptomics with network toxicology yielded 9 candidate genes and 15 shared KEGG pathways, which were mainly associated with neurocognitive function. SHAP prioritized hmox1, camkk2, and trem2 and molecular simulations predicted stable binding of KET to these proteins, supporting their role as candidate molecular initiating events. Gene expression changes correlated with altered glutamate, and GABA levels. Based on these multi‑level findings, we constructed a proposed adverse outcome pathway (AOP) network in which KET is predicted to bind to HMOX1, CAMKK2, and TREM2, which may contribute to oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and synaptic dysfunction converging on cognitive decline. This study provides evidence in adult zebrafish that sub-chronic exposure to environmentally relevant KET impairs cognition and proposes a multi‑target AOP network based on zebrafish data, supporting ecological risk assessment of KET as an emerging contaminant.

title: Advancing early detection of Alzheimer's disease: from established biomarkers to future innovations.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a major form of dementia, imposes an escalating global burden on public health and social care. Pathological changes in AD occur years before clinical symptoms, defining a prolonged preclinical phase. Currently, there is no effective treatment exist for late-stage AD, making early diagnosis and intervention indispensable, in which biomarkers play a pivotal role. While cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and positron emission tomography (PET) biomarkers improved AD diagnostic accuracy, their clinical application is limited by invasiveness, high costs. Advances in ultrasensitive immunoassay technologies has rendered peripheral blood biomarkers easily accessible, cost-effective, minimally invasive, and suitable for continuous monitoring, offering noval opportunities for AD screening, diagnosis and progression tracking. Additionally, non-invasive body fluids including saliva, urine and tears are being explored as potential biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven multimodal fusion, integrated with large-scale multimodal computing frameworks, significantly improve the accuracy of early AD diagnosis. Recent studies have identified a series of promising synaptic and neuronal biomarkers, such as neurofilament light chain (NFL), neurogranin (Ng), β-secretase 1 (BACE1) and synaptosomal-associated protein 25 (SNAP-25). Inflammatory mediators and genetic factors also contribute to AD pathological evaluation. This review systematically characterizes biomarker profiles of emerging non-invasive carriers (saliva, urine and tears). It further synthesizes cohort-derived quantitative diagnostic metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity) of multimodal AD biomarkers and conducts head-to-head comparison to clarify their respective strengths and translational limitations, aiming to provide evidence-based insights for optimizing early AD screening and diagnostic strategies.

title: CoilDrop-MRI: Self-supervised physics-guided MRI reconstruction with coil dropout.
abstract: Self-supervised deep learning-based methods have shown great promise for accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction, achieving high image quality without requiring fully sampled data for training. These methods typically partition the acquired data into two disjoint subsets to construct input-target pairs for optimizing the reconstruction network. However, existing approaches perform this partition exclusively within the spatial frequency (k-space) domain, leaving the coil dimension unexplored. To enforce full exploitation of signal correlation across receiver coils, we propose CoilDrop-MRI, which applies coil-wise dropout to the input and uses the dropped data as training targets in a self-supervised framework. This method is integrated into unrolled architectures in both image-domain (SENSE) and k-space (SPIRiT) formulations. We further demonstrate its versatility by extending CoilDrop-MRI to multi-shot, phase-corrected diffusion MRI (dMRI) reconstruction. CoilDrop-MRI is extensively validated on multi-site, multi-field-strength (0.3T, 0.55T, and 3T), and multi-modality (T1-weighted, T2-weighted, T2-FLAIR, and dMRI) datasets and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised methods, achieving quality comparable to supervised reconstruction methods without requiring fully sampled reference training data. Moreover, CoilDrop-MRI exhibits strong data efficiency and robust generalization across imaging conditions, establishing it as a practical and versatile framework for self-supervised parallel MRI reconstruction.

title: The distribution of real-world gait speed and its relation to gait bout length in people with and without gait impairment.
abstract: Real-world walking has been suggested to consist of two distinct constructs: slower walking ensembled in short walking bouts, and faster walking during longer walking bouts. Here, we evaluated the presence of a bimodal gait speed distribution reflecting these constructs in people with and without gait impairment. Remote walking data were analyzed from four cohorts: healthy adults (n = 16), chronic stroke (n = 20), end-stage knee osteoarthritis (n = 21), and incomplete spinal cord injury (n = 16). Participants wore a sensor on each foot and one on the lower back for three days. Gaussian mixture modeling was used to characterize each individual's gait speed distribution from all recorded strides. Bimodality was quantified using Ashman's D, with D > 2 indicating well-separated components. For participants with D > 2, bout lengths were compared between the slower and faster component. Well-separated components were found in 12 out of 73 participants (16%), with no evident differences between people with and without gait impairment. Overall, mean gait speed increased while variability decreased with longer bout length. Among participants with bimodal distributions with D > 2, bout lengths did not differ significantly between components (slow speed component: 11 [IQR: 7.5, 31.8] strides vs. fast speed component: 34.5 [IQR: 20.8, 122] strides; p = 0.056). Real-world gait speed distributions were typically not bimodal, and gait bout length could not explain bimodality. Together, our findings do not support the idea that distinct components of the gait speed distribution reflect short versus long walking bouts.

title: Adult Attention Deficit-Hyperactivity Disorder.
journal: The New England journal of medicine
abstract: Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a medical condition that is present in approximately 2.5% of adults worldwide and manifests in a variety of different ways across the lifespan. Adults with ADHD often have coexisting psychiatric disorders such as anxiety, mood, sleep, substance use, and personality disorders and are at increased risk for coexisting somatic conditions such as obesity, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and immune and inflammatory conditions. Hence, such adults may be seen by clinicians providing care for a wide range of psychiatric and somatic conditions. Nevertheless, ADHD remains unrecognized and undiagnosed in many persons. Assessment requires interviewing of the patient for core ADHD symptoms, coexisting conditions, and their functional effects, which can be facilitated by using standardized rating scales. Key components of treatment are psychoeducation and psychostimulant or nonstimulant medication, mostly in combination with psychosocial interventions and lifestyle guidance.

title: A Wolf in Disguise: Tuberculous Spondylitis Masquerading as Modic Changes With Reactivation After Epidural Steroid Injection - A Case Report.
abstract: Epidural steroid injections (ESIs) are commonly used for chronic low back pain but can rarely lead to serious infectious complications. Reactivation of latent tuberculous spondylodiscitis after ESI is uncommon. Our case highlights diagnostic challenges of underlying spinal infection prior to interventional pain procedures. A 43-year-old woman presented with low back and radicular pain. There were no constitutional symptoms, and baseline laboratory findings were unremarkable. Lumbar magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed Modic-type degenerative changes and nerve root compression. A transforaminal ESI was performed for presumed lumbar radiculopathy, but the pain persisted. Three weeks later, contrast-enhanced MRI revealed findings consistent with spondylodiscitis. Computed tomography-guided biopsy confirmed tuberculous spondylodiscitis, and antituberculosis therapy was initiated, leading to clinical improvement before any complications developed. Spinal tuberculosis may masquerade as degenerative Modic changes and may become clinically apparent following ESI. Persistent or worsening pain after spinal intervention should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.

title: Combining Pharmacological Therapy and Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection Resulted in Clinical Improvement in Bilateral Arterial-Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: A Case Report.
abstract: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) results from compression of the brachial plexus and/or the subclavian vessels. Botulinum toxin (BTX) has been shown to be useful in TOS both as a predictor of surgical outcome and as a therapeutic option. We present the case of a 21-year-old woman with a rare form of bilateral TOS with combined arterial and neurogenic involvement. After surgical treatment on the right side, the patient developed symptoms on the left side. We adopted a multimodal therapeutic approach that effectively reduced her symptoms and improved her quality of life. Our case suggests that alleviating neurovascular compression with BTX, together with pharmacological agents that modulate pain pathways, may lead to clinical improvement, even in complex and poorly documented cases of TOS.

title: Preoperative Sedation via Cecostomy Tube in an Autistic Adolescent: A Case Report.
abstract: Preoperative sedation of autistic children is frequently complicated by challenges in communication, sensory processing, and participation in medical care. We report a 40-kg, 13-year-old autistic boy with a preexisting cecostomy tube for chronic constipation, in whom previous oral and intramuscular sedation had failed due to agitation and physical aggression. Midazolam 10 mg (0.25 mg/kg) and ketamine 200 mg (5 mg/kg) were administered via cecostomy tube, producing sedation within 20 minutes. Dental rehabilitation under general anesthesia proceeded uneventfully. Cecal administration of sedatives may be a feasible option when conventional routes are poorly tolerated, although absorption, dosing, and reproducibility remain uncertain.

title: Lipid Chemistry beyond the Bilayer: Roles for Nonbilayer Lipids in Biology, Disease, and Delivery.
abstract: Cell membranes are composed of both bilayer and nonbilayer lipids, whose molecular shape and interactions support or oppose their packing into flat bilayer sheets. While the role of the former in maintaining membrane structural integrity is clear, a growing body of data highlights the importance of nonbilayer lipids in membrane function, including fission and fusion processes in trafficking, and the dynamics of membrane-associated proteins. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of nonbilayer lipids and their roles in membrane biology, disease, and drug delivery. First, we introduce the lipid chemistry that gives rise to intrinsic curvature and curvature elastic stress (CES), and we survey the chemical diversity of nonbilayer lipids across organelles and cell types. Second, we discuss relevant methodological advances for characterizing the physicochemical properties of nonbilayer lipids, including X-ray scattering, lipidomics, and molecular dynamics. We then examine how nonbilayer lipids contribute to membrane fusion and fission and how the CES they generate modulates membrane protein localization and function. Next, we consider how the biophysical principles governing nonbilayer lipid behavior can inform the rational design of lipid nanoparticle formulations for therapeutic delivery. Finally, we explore how cells regulate lipid intrinsic curvature as a distinct homeostatic parameter and discuss the implications of its dysregulation in liver disease, neurodegeneration, and mitochondrial dysfunction. We highlight developments in methods spanning the interface between chemistry and biology that can help investigate the function and regulation of nonbilayer lipid chemistry, with far-reaching potential to answer questions in human health, disease, and drug delivery.

title: Neurodevelopmental Blueprint in Gliomas: Toward an Ontogenetic Multimodal Integrated Therapy.
journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
abstract: Neuroepithelial tumors, including diffuse gliomas and embryonal neoplasms, remain among the most lethal cancers despite major advances in molecular diagnostics and some novel targeted therapies for subsets of patients. A persistent barrier to progress is the lack of a unifying framework that integrates their cellular hierarchy, spatial heterogeneity, and distinctive patterns of progression. In this review, we synthesize converging evidence that neuroepithelial tumor biology represents a pathologic re-enactment of brain ontogeny. Integrating molecular, single-cell, histoarchitectonic, and anatomic observations, we propose that neoplastic transformation, aberrant lineage commitment, and dedifferentiation mirror and invert physiological ontogenetic trajectories. This ontogenetic logic provides a coherent explanation for key hallmarks of neuroepithelial tumors, including intratumoral mosaicism, directional anatomic spread, and the emergence of therapy-resistant tumor-propagating cell states. Ontogenetic multimodal integrated therapy is an anatomy-guided strategy that aligns neurosurgery, radiotherapy, and pharmacotherapy with tumor stage and ontogenetic architecture. By shifting emphasis from radiologically visible tumor bulk to compartment-based developmental logic, this framework offers testable hypotheses and a clinically oriented paradigm for diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal monitoring in patients with neuroepithelial tumors.

title: Association Between Epilepsy and Young-Onset Dementia: Nationwide Data From France and Sweden.
abstract: Epilepsy is linked to late-onset dementia, but evidence for young-onset dementia (YOD; <65 years) is limited. We assessed the epilepsy-YOD association in France and Sweden and YOD risk after midlife epilepsy. We conducted 3 nationwide analyses. A French nested case-control analysis included patients with incident YOD aged 40-64 years, diagnosed between January 1, 2016, and December 31, 2018. Index date was the first YOD-related health care event; controls were risk-set matched on age, sex, and region. A Swedish nested case-control replication included patients with YOD diagnosed between January 1, 1987, and December 31, 2016, with matched controls. In both studies, epilepsy-related diagnoses and antiseizure medication (ASM) dispensations were assessed up to 10 years before index date. Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated with conditional logistic regression. A French retrospective cohort included adults aged 30-55 years with incident epilepsy in 2008, matched to individuals with prevalent epilepsy before 2008 or no epilepsy. The cohort index was the first ASM reimbursement in the incident epilepsy group or the matched date for comparators. Follow-up ended at YOD, death, or 10 years. We estimated 10-year cumulative incidence and adjusted (comorbidities, deprivation) hazard ratios (HRs), treating death as a competing event. Sensitivity analyses included lagged entry up to 5 years. Case-control studies included 11,360 cases and 113,600 controls in France and 16,433 cases and 164,330 controls in Sweden. In France, 12.5% of YOD cases vs 1.2% of controls had previous epilepsy-related codes (adjusted OR 3.76, 95% CI 3.42-4.14), and 27.3% vs 10.3% had ASM dispensations (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.36-1.52). The French cohort included 12,901 individuals with incident epilepsy, 64,083 with prevalent epilepsy, and 129,010 without epilepsy (mean age 44.0 years; 55.5% female participants). Ten-year cumulative YOD incidence was 2.20% (95% CI 1.94-2.48) with incident epilepsy (adjusted HR compared with individuals without epilepsy 6.02, 95% CI 4.98-7.26), 1.74% (1.64-1.85) with prevalent epilepsy (adjusted HR 5.38, 95% CI 4.64-6.25), and 0.21% (0.19-0.24) without epilepsy. Associations attenuated with longer lags but persisted beyond 5 years. Across 2 countries and complementary designs, epilepsy was strongly associated with YOD. Epilepsy conferred higher YOD risk in midlife, especially with multimorbidity, supporting epilepsy inclusion in YOD risk stratification and prevention.

title: The Brain-Gut-Microbiome Axis: Exploring the Link Between Depression and Irritable Bowel Syndrome.
abstract: The brain-gut-microbiome system is an integrated communication network linking the central nervous system, enteric nervous system, immune pathways, and intestinal microbiota. Increasing evidence indicates that dysregulation of this bidirectional signaling system contributes to both gastrointestinal and psychiatric disorders. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a disorder of gut-brain interaction, and major depressive disorder (MDD) frequently coexist and share multiple biological and environmental risk factors. Advances in microbiome science, neuroimaging, and multi-omics technologies have revealed that microbial metabolites, neuroimmune signaling, and stress-responsive neuroendocrine pathways influence neural circuits regulating mood, visceral perception, and gastrointestinal function. These interconnected mechanisms may explain the high comorbidity between IBS and MDD and suggest that both conditions arise from disturbances across overlapping biological systems. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of genetic, neurobiological, and potential microbial contributors to IBS and depression, discuss emerging therapeutic approaches targeting the brain-gut-microbiome system, and highlight future directions for developing mechanistically informed treatment strategies.

title: An Agenda for Physiology in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.

Development of Enhanced Reviews of Psychological Changes After Stroke (ENRICH): A complex Intervention to Monitor and Support Self-Management of Post-Stroke Psychological Changes Within a Matched Care Model.
abstract: ObjectiveTo report the design and development of a complex intervention to monitor and support self-management of post-stroke psychological changes.DesignThe Medical Research Council framework for complex intervention research guided development work, which included a literature review, semi-structured interviews with stroke survivors (n = 26) and family members (n = 11), a Delphi survey with healthcare professionals and researchers (n = 42), and workshops with stroke survivors (n = 4), family members (n = 3), and healthcare professionals (n = 5).SettingStroke community care.ParticipantsStroke survivors, family members, healthcare professionals and researchers.InterventionThe Enhanced Reviews of Psychological Changes after stroke (ENRICH) programme is a brief intervention deliverable within the UK matched care model of post-stroke psychological support. It supports stroke survivors with mild to moderate cognitive changes, low mood, anxiety and fatigue by monitoring symptoms, providing personalised psychoeducation, and supporting self-management through three brief reviews at 1, 3, and 6 months. Those with more severe or persistent psychological changes are referred through local care pathways for specialist psychological input.Main measuresThe intervention is reported using the TIDieR checklist.ResultsThe logic model and programme theory suggest benefits for psychological wellbeing and quality of life, with stakeholder input likely to enhance acceptability and feasibility.ConclusionsENRICH has the potential to address gaps in UK post-stroke care for those with mild to moderate changes affecting cognition, mood, anxiety and fatigue when delivered within the matched care model. Feasibility testing is underway with future clinical effectiveness testing is planned.

title: [Not Available].
abstract: Proponer un marco teórico para un modelo basado en agentes (MBA) que simule el inicio del consumo de nicotina en adolescentes mexicanos y evaluar el efecto potencial de prohibir la publicidad y exhibición de productos de tabaco en puntos de venta (PPE). Material y métodos. Se desarrolló un MBA en NetLogo 6.4.0 con datos de 6 557 adolescentes de una cohorte (2015-2016). El modelo integra tres módulos: 1) características del agente (factores intrapersonales, como percepción de riesgo); 2) condiciones físicas y materiales (factores ambientales, como número de tiendas), y 3) atributos comunitarios (factores interpersonales, como consumo familiar). Se realizaron 100 iteraciones para la calibración y validación mediante el análisis de similitud estadística de las medias de las variables de la cohorte y el modelo. El modelo reprodujo las prevalencias observadas en la segunda medición: fumadores 8.06%, vapeadores 6.36%, usuarios duales 3.79% y no consumidores 81.78%. La prohibición en PPE redujo la prevalencia total, aumentando los no consumidores a 85.83%. El MBA calibrado reproduce adecuadamente la dinámica de consumo adolescente y permite estimar impactos regulatorios potenciales. Representa una herramienta útil para apoyar decisiones en políticas de control de nicotina juvenil, aunque requiere actualizarse con datos actuales y mayor número de levantamientos.

title: [Not Available].
abstract: Desarrollar un modelo ajustado a datos empíricos para evaluar las interacciones entre dos medidas regulatorias y su potencial impacto en el consumo de nicotina en adolescentes en México. Material y métodos. Se desarrolló un modelo basado en agentes parametrizado con datos longitudinales de 6 557 estudiantes de secundaria de tres ciudades mexicanas. Se calibró para reproducir las prevalencias finales de consumo sin diferencias significativas, validando su salida predictiva. Se simularon un escenario base (impuestos 2016 sin prohibición de exhibición) y cuatro experimentales: 1. Impuestos a 2025 sin prohibición; 2. Impuestos a 2025 con prohibición; 3. Impuestos a 3 pesos sin prohibición; y 4. Impuestos a 3 pesos con prohibición. Todos los escenarios redujeron el consumo total de nicotina vs escenario base (18.21%), con disminución máxima de -39.54% en escenario 4. Los fumadores disminuyeron consistentemente; el vapeo aumentó con impuestos solos (+25% en escenario 3) pero se redujo con prohibición de exhibición (-12.58% en escenario 2). La combinación sinérgica de mayores impuestos y prohibición de exhibición maximiza la reducción del consumo de nicotina en adolescentes.

title: Microtubules and nuclear pores position centromeres and genes in neural stem cells.
abstract: Chromatin's spatial organization is important for cell division, epigenetic memory, and gene regulation. Chromatin architecture is often reflected in nonrandom centromere positioning, which changes during development and disease. However, the mechanisms and functions of centromere positioning remain largely unknown. Here, we report that Drosophila neural stem cells cluster centromeres near the nuclear envelope, adjacent to the apical centrosome. This asymmetric centromere positioning persists throughout interphase but is lost in differentiated progeny. Asymmetric centromere positioning is regulated by microtubules from the apical centrosome connected to nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), generating a pulling force mediated by the motor protein Dynein and its binding partner Mushroom body defect. Lamin facilitates centromere-NPC binding, necessary for centromere positioning and clustering. We also find that the developmentally regulated genes hunchback and pendulin occupy specific nuclear regions, correlating with polarized centromere localization. We propose that fly neural stem cells translate their inherent polarity into stereotypical chromatin organization, potentially influencing cell-fate decisions and stem cell behavior.

title: Risk and protective factors of solitary cannabis use among Canadian secondary school students: findings from the COMPASS study.
journal: Health promotion and chronic disease prevention in Canada : research, policy and practice
abstract: Solitary cannabis use has become increasingly prevalent among youth in Canada and is linked to both mental and behavioural concerns. This study seeks to fill current gaps in the literature by examining the factors associated with solitary cannabis use to understand the complexities of specific contexts in which use occurs and improve prevention efforts targeted towards behaviours that are associated with greater health impacts and riskier behaviours. This study examined solitary cannabis use among a cross-sectional sample (n = 2899) of Canadian youth (11-18 years) who reported past 30-day cannabis use and participated in the COMPASS study in 2020-21. Using a stepwise approach, generalized linear mixed models were run to examine risk and protective factors associated with solitary use. A Bayesian imputation framework was used to address missing data. Sixty-six percent of students reported having used cannabis alone in the past 30 days. All substance use variables examined were strongly associated with solitary use. A preliminary interaction between school connectedness and flourishing was observed, suggesting school connectedness may offer modest protection against solitary cannabis use and vary across flourishing scores. Solitary cannabis use is common among Canadian youth and is associated with several other risk factors examined. These findings suggest that comprehensive prevention strategies that promote both flourishing and equitable school environments may be relevant to reduce solitary cannabis use and its associated risks. Future research should explore how behaviours may cluster with solitary use and employ longitudinal designs to understand how behaviours change over time.

title: γ-aminobutyric acid is associated with calcium, reactive oxygen species, and nitric oxide responses and enhanced cadmium tolerance in Salvadora persica.
abstract: γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) accumulates under stress, but its association with calcium (Ca2+), reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide (NO), and thiol responses during cadmium (Cd) exposure remains unclear in medicinal shrubs. Rooted Salvadora persica L. cuttings were grown in sand-soil substrate. Screening selected 50mg Cd kg-1 substrate and 0.5 mM root-applied GABA. Eleven treatments had five independent pots each. Ca2+-sensitive Fluo-3 AM and NO-associated DAF-FM DA fluorescence and H₂O₂ were assessed in separate, destructively sampled plants at five post-application times. The 0-min value was a post-application reference; probe fluorescence was not calibrated to analyte concentration. Pot means were independent units, with time treated as a between-pot factor. A core Cd × GABA × time model and a separate categorical endpoint model were specified. The exact p-values, adjusted q-values, and model diagnostics could not be verified without pot-level records. Correlation and principal component analyses were exploratory; no path model was fitted. Cd reduced shoot dry weight from 3.04 to 1.89 g plant-1 (37.8%) and increased malondialdehyde from 4.37 to 9.86 nmol g-1 FW (125.6%). Relative to Cd alone, GABA increased the shoot dry weight to 2.62 g plant-1 (38.6%) and reduced the malondialdehyde to 4.34 nmol g-1 FW (56.0%). GABA was associated with a 2.2-fold greater Ca2+-sensitive fluorescence response amplitude at 30 min and 2.7-fold greater NO-associated amplitude at 360 min. LaCl₃, EGTA, DPI, DMTU, and cPTIO attenuated GABA-associated protection. Inhibitor-only and rescue controls were absent, and inhibitor phytotoxicity pre-screening was undocumented. GABA also increased total phenolics from 22.77 to 26.54 mg GAE g-1 DW (16.6%) and flavonoids from 13.21 to 15.78 mg QE g-1 DW (19.5%) relative to Cd alone. GABA was associated with improved Cd tolerance and differences in sampled fluorescence, H₂O₂, and thiol responses. These data cannot establish a continuous signaling sequence, upstream GABA action, or target-specific pharmacological effects. The attenuation is compatible with network involvement and feedback, but pathway direction and pharmacological specificity require inhibitor-only controls, rescue experiments, and independent, well-controlled temporal validation in future studies.

title: Preclinical and first-in-human evaluation of VG-3927/SAR448851, an oral small-molecule TREM2 agonist for Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Microglial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis, with loss-of-function variants in the microglial receptor TREM2 as major risk factors for late-onset AD. We report VG-3927, an oral, CNS-penetrant small-molecule TREM2 agonist that engages the transmembrane domains of TREM2 and its adaptor DAP12 to promote higher-order receptor complex formation and downstream signaling. VG-3927 and tool compound VG-3909 exhibited (sub)nanomolar potency, cooperated with endogenous ligands including amyloid-β (Aβ), and restored signaling in disease-associated TREM2 variants. In human iPSC-derived neuron-microglia-astrocyte cultures, VG-3927 reduced inflammatory cytokines and markers of neuronal damage. In 5xFAD amyloidosis mice expressing the common variant of hTREM2 (5xFAD;hTREM2CV), VG-3909 induced neuroprotective transcriptional reprogramming of microglia, particularly in the plaque niche; enhanced Aβ phagocytosis; and boosted brain glucose metabolism. By contrast, a TREM2 agonist antibody, which may be sequestered by soluble TREM2 (sTREM2), failed to engage plaque microglia. In a first-in-human, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 trial (NCT06343636, n = 115), VG-3927 was well tolerated across single and multiple ascending doses of up to 140 milligrams. Pharmacokinetics supported once-daily dosing with high CNS penetration (CSF-to-unbound plasma ratio of 0.91). VG-3927 induced dose-dependent reductions in CSF sTREM2, a biomarker of target engagement, consistent across healthy and elderly participants and participants with AD, supporting further clinical development in AD under the new designation SAR448851.

title: Photomapping electrically coupled networks of the mature thalamus and cortex.
abstract: Electrical synapses are expressed ubiquitously across the brain and are crucial components of active neural circuitry and connectomes. Identification of coupled networks in living tissue is limited by technical demands of multiplexed recordings, and no dyes, fluorescent reporters, or genetic labels can now fill the gap. We introduce a novel method of identifying and quantifying electrical synapses, opto-δL, that combines focal photostimulation of soma-targeted opsins with a spike timing-based computation for the strength of electrical synapses to rapidly measure and map electrically coupled networks in vitro. We leverage opto-δL to show that coupled networks of the mature thalamic reticular nucleus extend as far as 100 micrometers, synapse promiscuously across genetic subtypes of neurons, and couple one to four neighboring neurons to each recorded hub cell. We applied opto-δL to cortical networks, where we found that somatostatin neurons were more strongly and prevalently coupled. These results highlight the broad potential of opto-δL to interrogate the identity and roles of electrical synapses in circuitry, behavior, and cognition.

title: An inspiration-off attractor supports the robust and flexible control of breathing.
abstract: Breathing is a fundamental motor rhythm necessary to sustain life. The rhythm and pattern of breathing arises from the coordination of a rostrocaudally extended ventral respiratory column (VRC) in the medulla. Although recurrent excitation is sufficient for rhythmic bursting in reduced in vitro preparations, comparatively less is understood about how inhibition and excitation interact with feedback circuits to generate the breathing rhythm in vivo. Here, we expand on the classical "inspiratory-off switch" model that inhibitory signaling from lung stretch afferent pathways plays a critical role in generating the breathing rhythm in vivo. We perform high-density extracellular recordings along the length of the VRC during optogenetic and physiological manipulations and apply computational analyses to characterize how these perturbations govern low-dimensional neural dynamics. We show that stimulation of GABAergic afferents of the nucleus of the solitary tract advance or delay breathing in a manner similar to, but quantitatively distinct from, inhibition local to the VRC. We use generative dynamical models to show that inhibitory activity controls respiratory activity through transient stabilization of an attractive region of the low-dimensional manifold corresponding to expiration. Together, these results propose an "inspiratory-off attractor" model that underlies network level control of breathing in vivo.

title: Vitamin D binding protein in ventral CA3 of the hippocampus drives stress-induced depression.
abstract: The ventral hippocampus plays a crucial role in regulating emotional and motivated behaviors. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its dysfunction in major depressive disorder (MDD) remain poorly understood. Here, we identified elevated expression of vitamin D binding protein (VDBP) in the hippocampi of chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-susceptible mice, which correlated with the severity of depression-like behaviors. Notably, VDBP up-regulation was specifically in ventral CA3 excitatory (vCA3CaMKIIα) neurons. CA3CaMKIIα VDBP overexpression led to inhibited neuronal activity, synaptic and dendritic impairments, and, ultimately, depression-like behaviors. Conversely, vCA3CaMKIIα-specific VDBP knockdown enhanced resilience to chronic stress. Mechanistically, VDBP directly interacted with PIK3R3 to inhibit the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway in a cell-autonomous manner, leading to excessive autophagy and subsequent neuronal dysfunction. Chemogenetic activation, intervention using the Akt-specific activator SC79, and site-specific mutation disrupting the VDBP-PIK3R3 interaction ameliorated vCA3CaMKIIα VDBP-induced depression-like phenotypes. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical involvement of vCA3CaMKIIα neuron-derived VDBP in stress-induced depressive pathology and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for MDD.

title: Local control of Cre-regulated genetic modeling in vivo using wireless implantable optoelectronics.
abstract: Effective modeling of chronic human diseases in vivo requires precise spatiotemporal regulation of molecular processes at defined tissue locations. Optogenetic and optoelectronic tools can provide such control but targeting internal organs such as the lungs remain challenging. To address this, we developed E-LightR-Cre recombinase, enabling precise, spatially restricted gene activation with no dark-state activity and robust blue light responsiveness. To achieve local activation of E-LightR-Cre in specific organ sites, we engineered wireless, fully implantable optoelectronic devices enabling focal illumination of murine lungs with no discernible organ damage. The size of the activated area is controlled by modulating light intensity and duration. Using implanted optoelectronic devices, we activated E-LightR-Cre in a selected area of mouse lungs and achieved local regulation of targeted genes. Light-regulated expression of the oncogenic KRas-G12D mutant in mouse lungs induced local formation of oncogenic lesions. These results show that our protein engineering and adaptable optoelectronic approaches enable facile application of optogenetic tools for locally controlled disease modeling in vivo.

title: Learning to infer transitively on a mental line in premotor cortex.
abstract: Transitive inference (TI) is a form of deductive reasoning that enables the derivation of unknown relationships among premises. It is hypothesized that this cognitive process relies on mapping stimuli onto a "mental line," a linear workspace organized by arbitrarily assigned ranks. However, its neural basis remains unclear: Does this mental line have a neural correlate and how is it learned? This study investigates the role of dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) in encoding the hypothesized mental line as monkeys acquire item relationships for motor decisions. Findings reveal that PMd multiunit activity organizes along a theoretically predicted direction, supporting a geometrical model that explains behavior. Moreover, a learning process is observed, where the mental line rotates to align with motor planning.

title: Spectral tuning and signaling of diverse and far red-sensitive rhodopsins in mantis shrimp eyes.
abstract: Stomatopod crustaceans (mantis shrimps) have extraordinary eyes with unmatched visual rhodopsin diversity, but their potential for broad color detection remains unclear. Here, we report that 17 rhodopsins, mostly from the midband eye region, are involved in color sensing and functionally diverse signaling via Gq/Gi coupling and describe the underlying mechanisms of spectral tuning. Two mid-wavelength rhodopsins preferentially absorb blue light and a majority of long-wavelength opsins absorb in the green range, but three absorb light beyond 600 nanometers, representing exquisite far red-sensitive animal rhodopsins. Several blue and red rhodopsins exhibit photoreversibility with opposite spectral shifts explained by retinal binding interactions, revealing unrecognized photochemical flexibility in stomatopod photoreception. Row-specific spectral sensitivity results from combining carotenoid filters with multiple individually tuned rhodopsins, altogether extending broad vision to the far-red spectrum.

title: SPRIZ (CCDC127) protein conserved in deuterostome animals is a rigid OMM-IMM tether that locally sets mitochondrial IMS volume.
abstract: The double-membrane nature of mitochondria generates an intermembrane volume through which ions, reactive oxygen species, and metabolites must flux to reach the matrix or cytosol, but whether this volume is a genetically specified structure remains unknown. We identify SPRIZ (spatial regulator of the intermembrane zone), the product of Ccdc127, a gene conserved across deuterostome animals. SPRIZ assembles into an ∼18-nanometer homodimeric tether anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and inserted into the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) through vertebrate-specific hydrophobic loops, physically spacing the two membranes and setting local intermembrane volume. Cryo-electron tomography of native mitochondria revealed rod-like densities spanning the intermembrane space (IMS), consistent with SPRIZ's predicted rigid coiled-coil architecture and membrane-spanning topology. In mouse liver, two-dimensional morphometry measured ∼3-fold expansion of IMS area with SPRIZ and ∼5.5-fold with lengthened mitochondrial artificial increaser of the IMS (MARTINI); 3D electron tomography confirmed MARTINI's greater OMM-IMM separation and normalized IMS volume. This expansion was functionally validated by increased 14C-mannitol accessibility to the IMS and by impaired mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. Constitutive Ccdc127/SPRIZ knockout produced viable mice and, in liver mitochondria, preserved overall ultrastructure but caused modest IMS expansion, consistent with loss of local OMM-IMM constraints that stabilize membrane geometry at discrete sites. We therefore identify IMS volume as a genetically encoded and tunable architectural parameter of vertebrate mitochondria. In this model, SPRIZ is a molecular spacing system that locally sets OMM-IMM separation, shaping the environment through which metabolites, ions, and signals diffuse and establishing local gradients within the IMS.

title: Cellular diversity in neural organoids is critical for neurodegenerative disease modeling.
abstract: Neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction are hallmarks of most neurodegenerative diseases. For organoids intended to model neurodegeneration, immune, and vascular cells should therefore be considered fundamental components, rather than optional additions.

title: Exogenous nitric oxide as an anti-infective agent.
abstract: Both before and after the discovery that the high-output isoform of nitric oxide (NO) synthase (iNOS; NOS2) contributes to control of many infectious diseases, investigators have been treating infections with exogenous NO or NO-related moieties. Here, we review the anti-infective potential of topically applied NO-releasing materials, systemically administered anti-infective drugs that generate NO-related moieties, and inhalation of NO gas. Evidence for the safety and efficacy of inhaled NO (iNO) at higher doses than typically used in cardiopulmonary medicine encouraged us to discuss prospects for iNO to help treat pulmonary infections, with a focus on tuberculosis.

title: Stroboscopic light stimulation safety within and beyond laboratory settings: Observational evidence and practical guidance.
abstract: Stroboscopic light stimulation (SLS) reliably evokes geometric visual hallucinations and, in some contexts, altered-state experiences. Its increasing use in research, public, recreational and exploratory clinical settings creates a need for proportionate safety guidance. The main concern is a visually triggered seizure in a susceptible individual; reported non-epileptic responses include discomfort or distress. We combined a retrospective survey of safety practices and reported events across four laboratories, provider-reported operational data from two commercial SLS platforms, and a focused review of photosensitivity and sensory intolerance. Laboratory contributors reported 20 non-serious events that interrupted or modified participation, with no reported seizures or syncopal episodes. One commercial provider reported nine medically important or otherwise notable events across approximately 3.8 million sessions. The other reported five such events across more than 400,000 sessions. Because commercial adverse-event capture was passive and the laboratory protocols and monitoring procedures were heterogeneous, these figures cannot be used to estimate incidence or establish screening effectiveness. This synthesis informed a provisional Sussex Strobe Safety Screening Questionnaire (4SQ) and a layered, context-specific risk-management approach. The resulting framework distinguishes non-serious tolerability concerns from the principal medical risk of a visually provoked seizure in a susceptible individual, and supports conservative monitored familiarisation exposure, immediate stopping procedures and systematic adverse-event surveillance. The predictive performance of the 4SQ and the effectiveness of these precautions require formal evaluation; absolute SLS risk remains uncertain.

title: Hypoxia-inducible factor 2α does not regulate cortical brain development.
abstract: Dynamic changes in physiological oxygen levels are crucial for proper cortical brain development. In this context, oxygen is important not only for its role in energy metabolism but also as a signaling molecule. While much is already known about its most prominent signaling factor hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-1α, little is known about its functionally similar isoform HIF-2α during cortical development. Therefore, we utilized HIF-2α conditional knock-out mice (Emx1 and Nestin driven), which were kept under maternal hypoxia (10% pO2), physioxia (21% pO2), or hyperoxia (75% pO2) starting at E14.5 for 48 h and analyzed their cortical development by immunohistochemistry at E16.5. The analysis of newborn neurons (BrdU+) and cortical layer IV (Tbr1+), V (Ctip2+), and upper layer neurons (Satb2+) revealed clear effects of oxygen, with hyperoxia particularly increasing the number of Ctip2+/Tbr1- layer V neurons in E16.5 fetuses. However, neither the number of newborn neurons nor the number of layer-specific neurons was affected by HIF-2α CKO. Similarly, oxygen-related effects on neural stem cells (NSCs) and neuroprogenitor cells were not mediated by HIF-2α in E16.5 fetuses. Contributing, in vitro expansion and stem cell maintenance of NSCs were accelerated by physioxia (3% pO2) compared to hyperoxia (21% pO2), without involvement of HIF-2α under either condition. In conclusion, oxygen modulates cortical development, but HIF-2α does not mediate these effects. Thus, oxygen-related changes in neurogenesis and cortical morphology appear to be regulated via HIF-2α-independent mechanisms.

title: Protection of beta-blocker and 5-hydroxytryptamine 1A receptor agonist on myocardial ischemia injury in rats by regulating the NLRP3/Caspase-1/GSDMD pathway.
abstract: To explore the effects and related mechanisms of a β-blocker combined with a 5-hydroxytryptamine 1A receptor (5-HT1AR) agonist on MI injuries in rats. TTC/Evans blue, H&E, Masson, and TUNEL staining were used to assess infarction area, pathological damage, fibrosis, and apoptosis in myocardial tissue. The ELISA kits were used to detect IL-1β and IL-18 levels. The immunohistochemical (IHC) staining was used in conjunction with qRT-PCR and Western blot to determine IL-1β, IL-18, NLRP3, pro Caspase-1, cleaved Caspase-1, GSDMD-FL, and GSDMD-N expression levels. In myocardial tissue, the β-blocker combined with the 5-HT1AR agonist effectively reduced infarction size, mitigated pathological injury, alleviated fibrosis, and prevented apoptosis. Meanwhile, the β-blocker combined with the 5-HT1AR agonist downregulated IL-1β and IL-18 levels in serum and myocardial tissue. Notably, although it barely altered the expression of the pyroptosis precursor proteins pro Caspase‑1 and GSDMD‑FL, the combined therapy strongly suppressed the mRNA and protein levels of NLRP3, cleaved Caspase‑1, and GSDMD‑N, and reduced the ratios of pro Caspase‑1/cleaved Caspase‑1 and GSDMD-FL/GSDMD-N in myocardial tissue. β-blocker combined with the 5-HT1AR agonist relieves MI injuries by suppressing the NLRP3/Caspase-1/GSDMD pathway.

title: Smoke characteristics of conveyor-belt fires in U-shaped belt-conveyor roadways under different ventilation velocities.
abstract: To elucidate the smoke characteristics of conveyor-belt fires in U-shaped belt-conveyor roadways under different ventilation velocities, small-scale combustion experiments were conducted using PVG1250S flame-retardant conveyor-belt specimens. A PyroSim model of a U-shaped roadway was subsequently developed to examine smoke transport under different ventilation velocities and prescribed thermal-source intensities. The results show that, as the ventilation velocity increased from 0.4 to 1.6 m/s, the peak CO concentration at the monitoring point decreased from 453 to 175 ppm, whereas the peak flow-rate-corrected CO transport index increased by 54.43%. The fixed-point temperature response was non-monotonic and reflected the combined effects of combustion fluctuation, smoke-layer position, buoyancy, and convective transport. Numerical simulations further reveal that buoyancy dominates smoke movement under low-velocity ventilation, promoting upstream back-layering of hot smoke along the roof and local accumulation of heat and CO near the fire source. As the ventilation velocity increases, the longitudinal airflow increasingly suppresses and entrains the fire plume, thereby weakening upstream back-layering while enhancing smoke transport toward the downstream roadway, working face and connecting roadway. Based on the composite smoke-response index, the scenario-specific characteristic transition velocity associated with a marked reduction in long-distance upstream smoke back-layering was approximately 2.24 m/s, with a transition range of 2.0-2.4 m/s under the prescribed 4800 kW thermal-source sensitivity scenario. The results provide a reference for understanding smoke redistribution and ventilation effects in U-shaped belt-conveyor roadways under comparable source, geometric, and ventilation conditions.

title: Cerebrospinal fluid penetration of new antibiotics in the treatment of central nervous system infections.
abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial infections present significant challenges to the management of central nervous system (CNS) infections, particularly in neurosurgical patients and those with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) diversion devices. Achieving adequate CNS exposure is complicated by variable blood-brain barrier permeability and physiological changes, and CSF concentrations are not reliably predicted by plasma concentrations. Several new antibiotics have been introduced in response to rising MDR rates. To date, none are licensed for CNS infections, and data on CSF penetration and clinical utility are limited. Evidence describing CSF penetration of new antibiotics is limited and largely derived from small pharmacokinetic studies and case reports, predominantly in post-neurosurgical meningitis and ventriculitis. ?-Lactams (BL) such as cefiderocol, and the ?-lactam/?-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) combinations ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam and sulbactam-durlobactam, have achieved target CSF concentrations in individual cases, particularly with meningeal inflammation and intensive dosing. Predictors of adequate penetration are poorly defined, limiting identification of patients most likely to benefit, and the role of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) remains uncertain. Lipoglycopeptides and newer tetracyclines generally demonstrate low CSF penetration after systemic administration, with sparse clinical data supporting their use. CSF exposure to new antibiotics is highly variable, inconsistently achieves pharmacodynamic targets, and cannot be reliably inferred from plasma concentrations. Limited evidence suggests that BLs and BL/BLI combinations may have utility, whereas newer lipoglycopeptides and tetracyclines do not. Prospective studies and multicentre registries are required to better define CNS exposure, clarify the role of TDM, and inform practice.

title: The role of matrix metalloproteinases in Alzheimer's disease and small vessel disease.
abstract: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are a family of enzymes participating in maintenance and remodeling of the extracellular matrix. Their many types are involved in diverse, sometimes contrasting physiological processes, and they are ubiquitously present throughout the CNS. In this mini-review we focused on MMP-2, MMP-3, MMP-9, and MMP-14, highlighting their importance in pathways linked to Alzheimer's disease and small vessel disease. Despite overlapping roles in modulating brain-blood barrier impairment, neuroinflammation, and the accumulation of disease-specific proteins like amyloid-β and tau, they show somewhat distinct expression patterns in different cells and differ in their primary influences on disease mechanisms. Although our knowledge is still very limited, there is evidence linking them to imaging manifestations of cerebral vessel disease and suggesting they could be a target for therapeutic interventions.

title: Identifying drugs associated with Alzheimer's disease risk using machine learning-assisted signal detection.
abstract: BackgroundSeveral Alzheimer's disease (AD) clinical trials currently focus on drug repurposing. Machine learning (ML)-based pharmacoepidemiological approaches may help identify candidate drugs for trials.ObjectiveWe applied an ML-based signal detection method to identify drugs associated with AD risk.MethodsUsing Finnish nationwide register-based data, we defined drug exposure at both subgroup and drug substance levels according to the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification. Three binary embedded variables were calculated for each drug based on the frequency of dispensations over three years, starting 10 years before the index date. An algorithm combining subsampling and lasso-logistic regression was applied, with 500 replications for each drug exposure variable. Drug variables with a selection percentage (SP) ≥ 70% across replications were considered as signals. The average beta describes the direction and strength of the association.ResultsThe study population comprised 43,926 AD cases and 43,926 matched controls. The mean age was 80.3 years in both groups, and 65% of participants were women. Four drug subgroups and three individual drugs were associated with a lower risk of AD, whereas 14 subgroups and 11 individual drugs were associated with a higher risk. Drugs associated with decreased AD risk belonged to cardiovascular drugs: antihypertensives affecting the renin-angiotensin and diuretics.ConclusionsThe identified associations are consistent with established risk factors of AD and support the importance of effective hypertension management in AD prevention. Further studies are needed to evaluate whether antihypertensive drugs may exert neuroprotective effects and represent viable candidates for drug repurposing in AD.

title: Peptide signaling in the paraventricular thalamus is essential for disrupted adult reward behaviors consequent to early-life adversity.
abstract: Early-life adversity (ELA) is strongly linked to emotional disorders characterized by dysregulated reward behaviors. However, the mechanisms by which transient neonatal experiences generate enduring, sex-specific alterations in brain function remain unresolved. Paraventricular thalamus (PVT) neurons are selectively activated during ELA and contribute to disrupted adult reward behaviors. Here, we explore the molecular mechanisms behind these enduring, sex-specific disruptions. Combining activity-dependent genetic labeling with translating ribosome affinity purification, we find distinct gene translation programs in ELA and control mice of both sexes. Notably, the receptor for the neuropeptide corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor type 1 (Crhr1), is differentially expressed across rearing and sex in response to reward. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Crhr1 deletion exclusively in early-life-activated PVT neurons normalizes reward behaviors in both male and female adult ELA mice. Thus, CRHR1 signaling in adult PVT neurons activated by ELA is a required and potentially targetable mechanism underlying sex-specific, ELA-induced disruptions of reward behaviors.

title: Corrigendum to "Depression: higher temporal variability of the functional connectivity of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and hippocampal system" [NeuroImage: Clinical 52 (2026) 104073].
Disarming CH25H to clear α-synuclein.
abstract: α-Synuclein (α-Syn) accumulation is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD). Zhang et al. identify cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (CH25H) as an astrocytic inhibitor of p62-dependent α-Syn degradation.
