Disrupting the CH25H-p62 interaction facilitates α-Syn clearance via autophagy and improves PD-like phenotypes, suggesting a previously unrecognized nonenzymatic function for CH25H with therapeutic potential.

title: Resilience and vulnerability in the midbrain dopamine system during aging.
abstract: The midbrain dopamine system is integral to movement, reward, and motivation, and its dysfunction underlies a range of brain disorders. Age is a primary risk factor for many of these disorders, yet systematic analysis of how the dopamine system changes during healthy aging remains relatively understudied. In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. Elucidating these neuroadaptive mechanisms could offer a path toward preserving dopamine neuron function across the lifespan and potentially preventing age-related neurodegeneration.

title: Corrigendum to "Actigraphy-based sleep outcomes in substance use disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis" [Sleep Med Rev 88, 102297].
Utility of Blood Neutrophil to Diagnose Bacterial Infections under Satralizumab Treatment for Aquaporin-4 Antibody-positive Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder: A Report of Two Cases.
abstract: Satralizumab is an anti-interleukin-6 receptor biologic that may mask bacterial infections. We report two patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder who developed afebrile bacterial infections with normal C-reactive protein levels during satralizumab treatment. During non-infectious periods under satralizumab treatment, the neutrophil count and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio decreased, whereas the neutrophil change ratio, defined as the ratio of present to previous neutrophil counts, did not. At the time of infection, these variables were elevated compared to the intra-individual confidence intervals during non-infectious periods. These cases indicate the utility of neutrophil-related parameters in diagnosing bacterial infections during satralizumab treatment.

title: Sleep-related Brain Activity in an Arousal-reducing Agent-induced Mouse Model Evaluated with fMRI.
journal: Magnetic resonance in medical sciences : MRMS : an official journal of Japan Society of Magnetic Resonance in Medicine
abstract: Functional MRI (fMRI) has been established as a technique for capturing functional changes based on brain activity and is widely used to evaluate various diseases and physiological conditions. However, studies that systematically evaluate functional brain networks during arousal-reducing agent-induced sleep in mice by using resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) are limited. This study aimed to compare and analyze whole-brain functional connectivity (FC) and reorganization patterns of large-scale brain functional networks in the mouse brain during arousal-reducing agent-induced sleep, focusing on arousal-reducing agents acting on different arousal regulatory systems. Sixteen healthy male C57BL/6JmsSlc mice (aged 16.4 ± 8.7 week) were used in this study. The mice were assigned to 4 groups: control, zolpidem (20 mg/kg), lemborexant (40 mg/kg), and dexmedetomidine (75 μg/kg). rsfMRI was performed using a 9.4T MRI system equipped with an 86 mm volume transmit coil and an 8-channel receive-only coil (Bruker BioSpin, Ettlingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany). After head post-surgery and habituation, blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) images were acquired using a gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (GRE-EPI) sequence (TR/TE = 1500/14 ms). Each mouse underwent six 10 min imaging sessions. fMRI data were preprocessed using Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM12; Wellcome Centre for Human Neuroimaging, London, UK) and analyzed using the CONN FC toolbox (McGovern Institute for Brain Research, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA). ROI × ROI FC matrices were calculated for each fMRI session. Group differences were assessed using linear mixed-effects models that accounted for repeated measurements within animals, individual variability, and age differences among groups. Compared to the control group, the zolpidem group showed the smallest overall differences, whereas the dexmedetomidine group showed the largest differences. Furthermore, although relatively similar trends were observed between the groups in the distribution of mean correlation coefficients within each network, different trends were observed between the networks. In addition to network reorganization associated with the sleep-inducing state, which is commonly observed regardless of the arousal-reducing agent type, distinct network changes exhibiting arousal-reducing agent-specific connectivity patterns were observed.

title: Time2: A Framework for the Neural Dynamics of Visual Perception.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Whenever we look at an object, we seem to perceive it immediately. However, this is not the case for two reasons. First, it takes hundreds of milliseconds for the brain to process visual information reaching the retina. Second, perceiving an object requires fixating it for some duration-typically hundreds of milliseconds-during which the retina continuously receives new visual information. These facts together imply that visual information is both processed and received through time. These two temporal facets of perception, which we term processing time and stimulus time, are often conflated in the literature, and rarely considered together in experiments. Here, we argue that, to obtain a more complete portrait of visual perception and further constrain models of vision, it is essential to consider and measure both temporal facets simultaneously. We present a new method designed to do so that is based on reverse correlation: Time2 We show that this method allows us to precisely characterize many neural phenomena, including rhythmic perception, predictive processing, and coarse-to-fine sampling.

title: Voluntary movement initiation is associated with cardiac input in Libet's task.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: ​​The relationship between motor intention and initiation of voluntary movement remains a fundamental topic in neuroscience, originating from the seminal framework of B. Libet, introduced in 1983. Libet's paradigm significantly influenced discussions on intentionality, motor control, and free will. However, methodological critiques continue to challenge its interpretations, specifically the accuracy and validity of the 'urge to move' phenomenon. One understudied factor in this debate is the potential influence of interoceptive signals-such as cardiac activity-in shaping the experience of motor intention and movement initiation. In our study, we addressed this gap by examining whether cardiac signals modulate participants' experience of the 'urge to move', using behavioural and electrophysiological measures in 39 healthy human participants (17 males and 22 females) performing Libet's task. Crucially, when participants were asked to follow the 'urge to move', their button press timings were predominantly aligned with the diastolic phase of the cardiac cycle, indicating cardiac modulation of movement initiation. However, analysing heart evoked potential (HEP) amplitudes as a measure of cardiac input perception, we observed no differences in HEP amplitudes associated with changes in introspective demands during the task in both source and sensor spaces. Our results suggest that implicit perception of cardiac signals biases voluntary action initiation in Libet's task, independently of cortical interoceptive markers. These findings have implications for models of motor preparation, intentionality, and the bodily basis of voluntary action, challenging conventional interpretations of motor intention and informing debates on volition and interoception.Significance Statement Our study provides evidence that implicit perception of cardiac signals influences movement initiation in Libet's task. We demonstrate, for the first time, that when attending to the 'urge to move', participants tended to initiate voluntary movements during the diastolic phase of the cardiac cycle. These findings challenge traditional views on factors affecting motor initiation in Libet's task, suggesting the relevance of interoceptive processing. By highlighting the role of cardiac input in experiencing motor intention, our findings expand on existing debates on volition, agency, and free will, further underscoring the importance of integrating bodily signals into these theoretical frameworks.

title: Machine Learning Framework for Integration of Video and EEG Reveals Distinct Seizure Phenotypes in Mouse Models of Epilepsy.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Video-electrocorticogram (VEEG) recordings are the gold-standard diagnostic tool for detecting and characterizing seizures in rodent models of seizure and epilepsy. Manual/visual scoring remains the prevailing strategy despite significant limitations. Alternatively, automated and semi-automated analyses have been applied to either EEG or video features alone but integrating these disparate data forms presents a challenge that has not been sufficiently addressed. Here, we introduce an integrated machine learning pipeline that jointly leverages EEG and behavioral video data to enable scalable and objective event classification. Integrated video-EEG analysis was initially validated using a well-established pharmacologically induced seizure paradigm in male mice, where overt generalized motor seizures provide a clear benchmark. We then tested the pipeline on a genetic mouse model of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) that displays a complex spike-wave discharge (SWD) seizure phenotype that poses significant challenges for traditional scoring methods. Machine learning-powered integrated analysis of video-EEG recordings outperformed unimodal EEG- or video-based approaches and performed favorably to experienced rodent EEG electrophysiologists while also uncovering distinct phenotypic relationships, including classes of atypical behavioral and typical non-behavioral SWD events. This framework provides a flexible tool for high-throughput, precise analysis of VEEG data, with potential to accelerate discovery in epilepsy and seizure research. Furthermore, this approach represents a generalizable strategy for the integration of diverse neurobehavioral time series data types.Significance Statement Seizure detection in animal models of epilepsy has relied heavily on manual analysis of video-EEG recordings, a process that is slow and subjective. We present a machine learning pipeline that integrates EEG and video data from mice to classify seizures with high accuracy. This work was validated across two models, first a pharmacologically induced generalized seizure model, and second, a spontaneous spike-wave discharge (SWD) model in genetic epilepsy. Our approach detected events missed by human reviewers and revealed previously uncharacterized SWD subtypes distinguished by their behavior. By combining open-source tools in a flexible framework, this work lowers the barrier to high-throughput, unbiased seizure phenotyping, and also offers a broadly applicable strategy for linking neural activity to behavior in neuroscience research.

title: Cerebellar climbing fibers signal flexible, rapidly adapting reward predictions.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Classical models of cerebellar computation posit that climbing fibers (CFs) operate according to supervised learning rules, correcting movements by signaling the occurrence of motor errors. However, recent findings suggest that in some behaviors, CF activity can exhibit features that resemble the instructional signals necessary for reinforcement learning, namely reward prediction errors (rPEs). Despite these initial observations, many key properties of reward-related CF responses remain unclear, thus limiting our understanding of how they operate to guide cerebellar learning. Here, we have measured the postsynaptic responses of CFs onto cerebellar Purkinje cells using two-photon calcium imaging in mice of both sexes to test how CFs respond to learned stimuli that either do or do not predict reward. We find that CFs can develop generalized responses to similar cues of the same modality, regardless of whether they are reward predictive. However, the extent of this generalization depends on temporal context, and generalization does not extend across sensory modalities. Further, learned CF responses are flexible, and can be rapidly updated according to new reward contingencies. Together these results reveal two properties of learned CF responses: their generalization across similar cues is graded by the temporal and sensory context in which the cues are learned, and, when reward contingencies are reversed, they update rapidly to track new learning rules.Significance Statement The cerebellum is best known for coordinating movement, and the climbing fiber teaching signals thought to instruct cerebellar motor learning were long thought to report movement errors exclusively. Recent work has shown that these instructional signals can also convey information about reward. Here, by recording from these climbing fiber inputs in mice learning which cues predict reward, we find that they carry flexible, context-sensitive reward predictions. Notably, these signals do not simply track which cue an animal should respond to: they generalize across similar cues depending on context, and they rapidly reorganize when reward associations change. These properties resemble those of midbrain dopamine neurons, the brain's canonical reward system. These findings reframe how cerebellar teaching signals contribute to reward-guided learning.

title: Microglial Presenilin-1 modulates neuronal function and memory-associated behaviors.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Microglial cells, the macrophages of the brain parenchyma, are increasingly recognized to play a key role in synaptic plasticity and function. Presenilin 1 (PS1) is an essential protein involved in learning and memory; the loss of neuronal Presenilin function causes cognitive deficits and impaired synapse plasticity in mice. Here we show memory enhancement in male mice lacking PS1 in microglia (PS1ΔMG). Leveraging high-throughput RNA sequencing with single-cell deconvolution-analysis, we estimate that PS1ΔMG increases Cd52-lo microglial population, a proliferative group enriched in AP-1 responsive genes; and increases chemokines Ccl7 and Ccl8 In silico prediction of binding partners showed that microglial CCL7 may act via inhibition of neuronal CCR5, a receptor known to negatively regulate learning and memory. By profiling active neuronal populations via PhosphoTRAP the data showed a non-autonomous cell effect of microglial PS1 by modulating genes involved in neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity. Ex vivo electrophysiology and in vivo calcium imaging in freely behaving mice confirm these effects with functional changes in CA1 hippocampus as seen by increased NMDA/AMPA ratios and increased amplitude of neuronal Ca2+ transients in freely behaving animals, respectively. Remarkably, PS1ΔMG mice exhibited increased memory retention in contextual fear conditioning and novel object recognition. Together, these data suggest a novel mechanism where microglial PS1 negatively regulates neuronal activity through modulation of NMDAR and memory-associated behaviors.Significance Statement Microglia are increasingly recognized as active regulators of neuronal function, yet the molecular mechanisms that constrain their influence on synaptic activity remain incompletely defined. This study identifies microglial Presenilin-1 (PS1) as a key regulator of neuron-microglia signaling that shapes synaptic transmission and learning. We show that loss of microglial PS1 shifts microglia toward a transcriptional and signaling state that enhances NMDA receptor-dependent synaptic activity and improves memory, demonstrating that microglial molecular programs can directly modulate neuronal excitability. These findings establish microglial PS1 as a physiological brake on circuit plasticity and reveal that altering microglial signaling alone is sufficient to influence cognition. Targeting microglial regulatory pathways may therefore provide new strategies to enhance synaptic resilience and cognitive function in brain disorders.

title: iGABASnFR Imaging Reveals that GABA Clearance is rapidly overwhelmed in the Cerebral Cortex.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Both phasic and tonic GABAergic activity in the cortex, is shaped by the clearance of GABA from the extracellular space by GABA transporters (GATs). However, estimates of the time-course of GAT activity from GAT currents, GABAA, and GABAB electrophysiological recordings range from tens of milliseconds to multiple seconds. These estimates may reflect receptor properties rather than extracellular GABA dynamics. Understanding how long GABA is free in the extracellular space is key to understanding how inhibition controls activity, but has been technically challenging. Here, we utilize the fluorescent GABA sensor, iGABASnFr, to enable us to optically assay extracellular GABA dynamics following bursts of synaptic activity. In the mouse cerebral cortex of either sex, we show that GABA rapidly disperses from release sites via diffusion, with very little role for active transport by GATs. Following diffusion from the sites of release, GABA then accumulates in the extracellular space, where GATs require hundreds of milliseconds to remove it. For areas of high density GABA release or during bursts of activity, this clearance is further slowed. Continued GABA release and summation in the extracellular space for bursts of activity contrasts with recorded Inhibitory post-synaptic current (IPSC) signals, which rapidly depress with additional stimuli, suggesting a disconnect between IPSCs and extracellular GABA. Lastly, the resulting extracellular accumulation of GABA can act hetero-synaptically by activating and/or desensitizing GABAA receptors. Together, this raises new questions about how GABAergic inhibition works to shape network function and suggests a spatiotemporal continuum of extracellular GABA.Significance Statement We use combined iGABASnFr neurotransmitter imaging, electrophysiology, and modeling to show that with trains of synaptic activity, GABA clearance is slowed and GABA rapidly accumulates in the extracellular space. Additionally, we demonstrate that GABA largely diffuses from release sites rather than being captured by GABA transporters and that these transporters have only a small role in shaping extracellular GABA dynamics in the mouse cortex. Lastly, we show that extracellular GABA accumulation can heterosynaptically desensitize GABAA receptors, modulating local phasic inhibition.

title: Deletion size and background genetic variation shape congenital heart disease phenotypes in 3016 individuals with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
Post-traumatic dementia: Advances in understanding neurodegenerative mechanisms.
journal: Chinese medical sciences journal = Chung-kuo i hsueh k'o hsueh tsa chih
abstract: Traumatic brain injury can trigger long-term neurodegenerative diseases beyond its devastating acute effects. This narrative review summarizes current understanding of the neurodegenerative mechanisms underlying post-traumatic dementia. Core mechanisms involve multiple pathophysiological processes: long-term dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier, which impairs the clearance of toxic proteins; diffuse axonal injury, leading topersistent disruption of axonal transport, dysregulation of calcium homeostasis, and Wallerian-like degeneration; and the abnormal deposition of key pathological proteins such as amyloid-β, hyperphosphorylation and propagation of tau protein, and dysfunctional TAR DNA-binding protein-43, all of which disrupt protein homeostasis. In addition, chronic neuroinflammation mediated by microglia and astrocytes acts as a critical link, continuously exacerbating synaptic damage and neurodegeneration through the release of pro-inflammatory factors. Genetic factors, such as the APOE4 allele, can significantly amplify these pathological processes. Collectively, this evidence indicates that traumatic brain injury is not an isolated acute event but rather initiates and accelerates a long-term, multifactorial neurodegenerative cascade, ultimately resulting in cognitive dysfunction. These insights provide important targets for the development of targeted intervention strategies.

title: Interpreting Lower Synaptic Vesicle Glycoprotein 2A Availability in Bipolar Disorder.
Zfp697/ZNF697 is an RNA-binding protein that modulates TGF-β1 signaling and hepatic inflammation in liver disease.
abstract: Liver diseases driven by metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and fibrosis such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and acute liver injury represent a growing global health burden. The zinc finger protein Zfp697 (ZNF697 in humans) is a newly identified regulator of inflammation and regeneration in skeletal muscle. Here, we characterize the role of liver Zfp697 and show that its expression is increased in multiple animal models of liver disease. Indeed, Zfp697/ZNF697 transcript levels show a strong positive correlation with several markers of liver inflammation and fibrosis. In line with that, in human and mouse hepatocytes TGF-β1 increases Zfp697 expression, which in turn regulates genes involved in TGF-β1 signaling, chemokine secretion, and immune cell recruitment. In mice, hepatocyte-specific Zfp697 deletion improves glucose tolerance and is associated with the absence of MASH-induced lean mass loss but does not confer uniform hepatoprotection. Biochemical purification of Zfp697 protein interactors and enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (eCLIP) analyses reveal that Zfp697 interacts with other RNA-binding proteins and associates with over 1,000 RNAs in mouse liver. Zfp697-associated RNAs include several transcript types, with a large representation of mRNAs which group in pathways related to transcriptional regulation, PI3K/AKT signaling, and cell differentiation. These findings identify Zfp697 as a novel RNA-interacting protein and modulator of TGF-β signaling in the liver and provide a basis for further investigation of its role in liver disease.

title: Deficiency of Synaptotagmin 9 in the Hippocampal Region Induces Synaptic Damage and Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson's Disease Mice via BDNF/TrkB Signaling.
abstract: Cognitive impairment is a prominent non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD) that severely affects patients' quality of life, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of hippocampal Synaptotagmin 9 (Syt9) in PD-related cognitive deficits. We found that Syt9 expression was significantly downregulated in the hippocampus of both MPTP-induced subacute PD mice and A53T α-synuclein transgenic mice, concomitant with cognitive impairment and synaptic damage. To determine causality, we performed hippocampal Syt9 knockdown and overexpression using AAV-mediated gene delivery. Syt9 knockdown exacerbated, while Syt9 overexpression alleviated, cognitive deficits and synaptic structural abnormalities in PD mice. Proteomic sequencing and pharmacological manipulations revealed that Syt9 may regulate the BDNF/TrkB signaling pathway at the protein level, likely by influencing BDNF vesicular transport, release, or stability. Intra-hippocampal BDNF supplementation rescued synaptic damage and cognitive impairment, whereas the TrkB antagonist ANA-12 reversed the protective effects of Syt9 overexpression. Collectively, our findings identify the Syt9/BDNF/TrkB axis as a key mechanism in PD-related cognitive impairment and suggest that targeting this pathway may offer a novel therapeutic strategy for PD.

title: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors in the prelimbic cortex modulate chronic neuropathic pain and comorbid generalised anxiety in a rainbow boa snake threat paradigm.
abstract: The prelimbic division (PrL) of the medial prefrontal cortex is implicated in the pathogenesis of generalised anxiety and chronic pain disorders. This study aimed to investigate the role of PrL N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor signalling in the comorbidity between neuropathic pain and psychiatric disorders. Male Wistar rats were exposed to the Enriched Polygonal Arena Snake-Evoked Panic Test involving confrontation by a constrictor snake. Neuropathy was induced by chronic constriction injury (CCI) of the ischiadicus nerve. Rats subjected to a sham surgical procedure were used as controls. Electrophysiological recordings were performed to assess PrL neuronal activity in CCI and sham-operated rats. Exposure to the threatening environment was conducted 21 days after surgery for 5 min following PrL cortical treatment with vehicle or LY235959 (2, 4, and 8 nmol). Neuronal activity in the PrL cortex was reduced in CCI rats. When confronted with a potential predator, threatened CCI rats exhibited increased emotional defensive responses accompanied by a decrease in mechanical paw withdrawal threshold (MWT), whereas sham-operated animals (without neuropathy) showed an increase in MWT following snake confrontation. Furthermore, NMDA receptor blockade in the PrL cortex with LY235959 reduced both defensive behaviours and mechanical allodynia in threatened animals. These findings suggest that NMDA receptor signalling in the PrL cortex plays a key role in the potentiation and maintenance of the comorbidity between anxiety/panic-like states and chronic neuropathic pain.

title: The ferroptosis-neuroinflammation feedback loop in traumatic brain injury: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of death and disability worldwide, with secondary injury processes such as ferroptosis and neuroinflammation adding to its detrimental effects. Recent studies reveal a profound bidirectional interaction. On one hand, inflammation drives ferroptosis by disrupting iron homeostasis through the IL-6/Janus kinase 2 (JAK2)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3)-hepcidin axis, impairing the system Xc-/glutathione (GSH)/GPX4 antioxidant system and promoting immune cell infiltration. Conversely, ferroptotic cells release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), including high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) and lipid peroxidation end-products like 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), which activate toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling and fuel a neuroinflammatory vicious cycle. We further discuss emerging therapeutic approaches targeting this axis, including ferroptosis inhibitors (Fer-1, Lip-1), dual-regulatory agents (Annexin A5, melatonin, and H2S), and exosome-based delivery systems, while highlighting translational difficulties presented by the BBB and complex time windows. This review presents a framework to comprehend the interplay between ferroptosis and inflammation and to guide the development of dual-targeted treatments in TBI.

title: Role of phasic activity of the substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons during voluntary movement: a case for context.
abstract: Despite decades of research the role of the dopaminergic neurons (DANs) of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) in movement and behaviour remains unclear and controversial. The classic model that equates tonic dopaminergic activity with permitting wanted movement and phasic activity with appetitive learning is no longer sufficient with the advent of evidence implicating phasic DAN activity with memory, novelty and saliency encoding, movement, exploration, and motivation. The aim of this review paper is to build a case that the appetitive and movement-related roles of phasic dopaminergic activity can be reconciled by the context in which the phasic activity is taking place. Specifically, we propose that SNc DAN phasic activity acts to integrate moment-by-moment motivational context with ongoing behaviour and thereby adds a motivational gain to contextually appropriate behaviours. We make this case by bringing together the findings of seminal works observing phasic SNc DAN activity at the onset of movement in motivated and unmotivated experimental paradigms, and optogenetic studies probing the causal effect of phasic dopamine (DA). Furthermore, we bring together evidence of phasic SNc DAN activity being responsive to changes in the novelty of an environmental stimulus and that its effect on behaviour may depend on the motivational nature of this stimulus. Finally, we propose possible circuits that might function to integrate memory into the motivational gain attributed to context-specific behaviours.

title: Pleiotrophin: a multifunctional regulator in neurodevelopment and neuropsychiatric diseases.
abstract: Pleiotrophin (PTN) is a heparin-binding growth factor that plays a pivotal role in neurodevelopment, neuroplasticity, and neuroinflammation. PTN signals through a multi-receptor network involving protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type ζ (PTPRZ1), syndecans (particularly syndecan-3), integrins, nucleolin, and neuropilin-1. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) has also been functionally linked to PTN signaling, although whether PTN directly binds and activates it remains debated. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in understanding the structure, distribution, and multifunctional roles of PTN in the nervous system, with a particular focus on its involvement in neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, anxiety, depression, and schizophrenia. Emerging evidence suggests that PTN exhibits context-dependent and often dual roles, both neuroprotective and pathogenic, depending on the disease stage and cellular microenvironment. This review highlights the potential of PTN as well as its receptors as therapeutic targets and underscores the direction for further research to elucidate its precise mechanisms in neurological and psychiatric conditions.

title: Lesions in the cerebellum impact cross-modal temporal predictions.
abstract: The cerebellum (CE) supports the encoding of the precise sensory event timing and the generation of temporal predictions. Here we investigated whether focal CE lesions impact temporal predictions in a cross-modal context. Individuals with CE lesion (n=9) and healthy-matched controls (HC) were presented with visuo-auditory stimulus pairs, presented in a temporally regular (predictable) or irregular (unpredictable) manner while EEG was recorded. We hypothesized cross-modal temporal predictions to be mediated by pre-stimulus cerebello-cortical beta-band (12-25Hz) activity. In turn, we expected HC, but not CE patients, to show a modulation of pre-stimulus beta power as a function of temporal prediction. HC showed greater pre-stimulus beta-band suppression presumably related to anticipation of sound onsets, and stronger post-stimulus delta-band (1-4Hz) power in the predictable than unpredictable condition. Furthermore, they displayed a significant modulation of pre-stimulus delta-beta cross-frequency coupling as a function of temporal predictability. These effects were not observed in the CE group, suggesting a deficit in temporal predictions. These results extend the role of cerebellar predictive timing from sensorimotor to motor-independent cross-modal temporal predictions.

title: Treatment-refractory autoimmune glial fibrillary acidic protein astrocytopathy: Clinical features, predictive models, therapy.
abstract: A subset of glial fibrillary acidic protein astrocytopathy experiences treatment-refractory disease course, yet the clinical and immunological features defining this subgroup remain incompletely characterized. Patients were classified as treatment-refractory (n = 23) or treatment-responsive (n = 30). Clinical, imaging, and outcomes were compared. For subgroup analyses, refractory patients were divided into three groups: no immunoadsorption/plasma exchange (IA/PE) (n = 9), IA/PE monotherapy (n = 4), and IA/PE plus rituximab (n = 10), with functional outcomes compared across groups. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) from refractory patients was applied to a passive transfer mouse model, and single-cell RNA sequencing was performed to explore underlying pathogenic mechanisms. The treatment-refractory group had higher proportion of the meningoencephalomyelitis phenotype (82.6% vs. 53.3%, P = 0.026) and more frequent disturbances of consciousness (65.2% vs. 30.0%, P = 0.011), paraplegia (78.3% vs. 33.3%, P = 0.001), and peripheral nervous system involvement (89.5% vs. 22.2%, P < 0.001). Refractory patients had elevated cerebrospinal fluid glial fibrillary acidic protein and neurofilament light chain levels. Refractory patients more frequently exhibited spinal cord lesions involving three or more segments (65.2% vs. 21.4%, P = 0.002). Disability at last follow-up was greater in the refractory group (median modified Rankin Scale score 3 vs. 1, P < 0.0001). Firth penalized regression model identified peripheral nervous system involvement as the independent predictor of treatment refractoriness (odds ratio = 10.74, P = 0.006). Among refractory patients, the IA/PE-plus-rituximab group had significantly lower long-term mRS scores than the no-IA/PE group (adjusted P = 0.031). GFAPA-IgG from refractory patients induced CD45+ cell infiltration in mouse brain. Single cell analysis demonstrated activation of complement and inflammatory pathways, with astrocytes adopting a pro inflammatory state. Treatment refractory disease is marked by severe central and peripheral nervous system injury. Convergent clinical and experimental evidence provides a rationale for B cell targeted therapies.

title: A homozygous GABRA2 variant associated with infantile spasms evolving to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome alters receptor gating.
abstract: Variants in GABAA receptor subunits are increasingly implicated in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Although GABRA2 variants have been associated with early-onset epilepsy, the functional consequences of individual variants, particularly those located outside canonical ligand-binding and transmembrane pore-forming regions, remain incompletely understood. We identified a homozygous GABRA2p.A407K variant in a patient with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS) evolving to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS). Functional effects were assessed using two-electrode voltage clamp in Xenopus laevis oocytes and whole-cell patch clamp recordings in HEK293T cells expressing α2β3γ2 GABAA receptors. A Gabra2p.A407K/A407K knock-in mouse model was generated to examine neuronal membrane properties, provoked seizure responses, and behavioral phenotypes. The p.A407K variant did not impair receptor trafficking but slowed receptor desensitization. In hippocampal slices from adult knock-in mice, CA1 pyramidal neurons exhibited a more depolarized resting membrane potential and were positioned closer to action potential threshold, while action potential threshold itself was unchanged. In a limited adult EEG cohort of Gabra2p.A407K/A407K mice, no spontaneous seizures or overt epileptiform activity were detected. However, mutant mice showed prolonged seizure duration following 6 Hz corneal stimulation. Behavioral analyses revealed increased locomotor activity and altered exploratory behavior. These findings show that a rare homozygous GABRA2 intracellular loop variant alters α2-containing GABAA receptor gating and produces measurable neuronal, behavioral, and provoked seizure-response effects in a knock-in mouse model. The model does not reproduce the full human developmental epileptic encephalopathy phenotype but supports the conclusion that p.A407K is functionally consequential and provides a platform for studying variant-specific effects of GABRA2 dysfunction.

title: Caffeine Consumption and Adolescent Mental Health: The Role of Sleep and Brain Structure.
journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
abstract: Caffeine is a widely consumed psychoactive substance, with use beginning during adolescence, a sensitive period of neurodevelopment. Despite its widespread, unregulated use, links between caffeine consumption and adolescent brain structure and mental health remain poorly understood. We examined the association between caffeine intake and brain structure in 9632 adolescents aged 9-11 years. Caffeine consumption (intake of coffee, tea and soft drinks) and mental health were assessed via self-report. Cortical thickness and surface area were derived from structural MRI scans. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between caffeine intake and brain measures. Structural equation modeling was used to test whether sleep duration and brain structure mediated the association between caffeine intake and mental health outcomes assessed at the 6-month and 18-month follow-up. Higher total caffeine intake was associated with lower total cortical surface area (B=-0.03,SE=0.01,p=.001) and lower surface area in 22 regions across four lobes, driven largely by soft drink consumption, with some additional associations emerging for coffee and espresso intake with cortical thickness. All associations were evident at consumption levels as low as one cup per week. Shorter sleep duration and lower surface area sequentially mediated the association between higher caffeine intake and greater mental health problems in the future. Findings highlight the need for evidence-based guidelines on adolescent caffeine consumption to support neurodevelopment and mental health.

title: Tyramine modulates synaptic transmission in vertebrate neuromuscular junction by releasing catecholamines and activating alpha-adrenergic receptors.
abstract: Tyramine is a biogenic amine whose role is closely linked to the sympathetic nervous system. Sympathetic axons densely innervate the neuromuscular junction regions of skeletal muscles. We hypothesized that tyramine might be the involvement in modulation of acetylcholine (ACh) release in the neuromuscular junctions. On the mouse Levator Auris Longus muscle it was found that tyramine enhances the loss of fluorescent false monoamine neurotransmitter FNN 511, preloaded into sympathetic varicosities located near the neuromuscular junctions. This indicates tyramine-induced release of endogenous catecholamines. Analysis of the ACh release demonstrated that tyramine decreases spontaneous exocytosis (estimated by the frequency of miniature endplate potentials) and evoked ACh secretion (assessed by the quantal content of the endplate potential). These inhibitory effects of tyramine were completely eliminated by doxazosin, an α1-adrenoreceptor blocker, but not SKF 86466, an α2-adrenoreceptor inhibitor. The negative action of tyramine on neuromuscular transmission was also manifested as a decrease in muscle contraction force during strong nerve activation. At the same time, tyramine did not inhibit the contractile responses to the direct muscle fiber stimulation. Finally, we obtained evidence of endogenous release of tyramine (and its derivative, octopamine) from the isolated neuromuscular preparation. Thus, tyramine can supress ACh release and, hence, contractile response to nerve activation probably by an indirect mechanism likely engaging the enhancement of endogenous catecholamine release and the downstream activation of α1-adrenoreceptors.

title: Extracellular flux analysis and proteomic profiling indicate ibogaine promotes synaptic plasticity and neural repair by a metabolic preconditioning mechanism.
abstract: We have examined how ibogaine may enhance synaptic plasticity and neural repair. Extracellular efflux analysis showed that ibogaine (3, 10 or 30 μM) produced a rapid (<5 minutes) and concentration-dependent suppression of mitochondrial function and glycolysis in mouse cortical neurons. Cell-based imaging demonstrated this metabolic inhibition was preceded by an elevation of the mitochondrial membrane potential and followed by increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species levels. Like ibogaine, which blocks potassium channels, mitochondrial Kv1.3 channel (mitoKv1.3) inhibitors produce concordant changes over a similar timeframe. Following treatment with ibogaine (3, 10 or 30 μM) for 4 hours, a marked concentration-dependent rebound of energy production occurred 20 hours later suggestive of metabolic preconditioning. Indeed, proteomic profiling showed that oral ibogaine (100 mg/kg) administration to female mice produced changes in spinal cord protein abundance indicative of increasing metabolic stress from 0.25-24 hours that resolved by 72 hours. This was accompanied by activation, inhibition and reactivation of synaptic plasticity and neural repair signaling pathways at 0.25, 4-24 and 72 hours, respectively. Hence, by inducing transient metabolic stress, ibogaine may re-open a neurodevelopmental window characterized by enhanced synaptic plasticity and neural repair. Ibogaine binds with high affinity to the sigma-2 receptor. Like mitoKv1-3 inhibitors and sigma-2 receptor ligands, ibogaine transiently elevated AMP-activated protein kinase (0.25 hours) and temporally suppressed mechanistic target of rapamycin and lipid synthesis pathways (0.25-24 hours) implicated in enhanced synaptic plasticity and neural repair. These findings suggest ibogaine rewires and repairs neural circuits by a metabolic preconditioning mechanism, perhaps involving mitoKv1.3 and the sigma-2 receptor.

title: Early post-sepsis innate behavioral changes in aged mice occur independently of detectable neuroinflammation.
abstract: Sepsis disproportionately causes long-term cognitive and functional impairments in elderly survivors, including deficits in activities of daily living and functional independence. The neurobiological mechanisms driving this vulnerability in the aged brain remain poorly understood. We tested whether the aged brain possesses a unique vulnerability to sepsis-induced impairment in the early post-acute recovery period. Polymicrobial sepsis was induced in young (3-months) and aged (18-months) mice via cecal slurry injection, with dosing adjusted for comparable acute illness severity. Behavioral assessments (learning, memory, locomotion, innate behaviors) were performed through Day 7 post-infection. On Day 8, brains were analyzed for inflammatory cytokines, glial activation, neuronal protein expression, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. Aged septic mice exhibited alterations in nest building and sociability, whereas young mice with comparable illness severity remained behaviorally resilient. The behavioral changes in aged mice occurred in the absence of broad systemic or neuroinflammation. Conversely, young septic mice maintained normal behavior despite significantly elevated systemic and neuroinflammation. Aged mice displayed signs of glial activation, neuronal protein modulation, and BBB permeability compared to young mice, but sepsis did not significantly exacerbate these markers in either group. Our findings demonstrate an age-dependent divergence in neurologic recovery after sepsis: while young mice exhibit behavioral resilience despite systemic and neuroinflammation, aged mice display alterations in innate behavior that are present even after the apparent resolution of acute illness. This suggests that the changes in innate behavior in the aged mice are not driven solely by sepsis-induced inflammation, but rather by a cumulative burden of age-related vulnerabilities, including microglial priming, astrocytic activation, and increased BBB permeability, that render aged brains unable to compensate for a severe acute physiological challenge.

title: CAP1 mediates chronic inflammatory pain-induced anxiety through cAMP/PKA/NF-κB signaling pathway in the anterior cingulate cortex of male mice.
abstract: A substantial subset of chronic pain patients suffers from comorbid anxiety, and this bidirectional exacerbation poses a major clinical challenge. Current pharmacotherapies have limited efficacy with notable side effects, underscoring the need for new targets. We successfully established a Complete Freund's Adjuvant (CFA) ‑induced chronic inflammatory pain model in male mice, which developed mechanical/thermal hyperalgesia, anxiety‑like behaviors, and Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC) synaptic plasticity abnormalities. RNA‑seq identified marked upregulation of ACC Adenylyl Cyclase‑Associated Protein 1 (CAP1). ACC CAP1 overexpression in naive mice selectively reduced mechanical pain and induced anxiety without affecting thermal nociception, whereas ACC CAP1 knockdown in CFA mice reversed anxiety and restored Excitatory/Inhibitory (E/I) balance while leaving pain thresholds unchanged. Mechanistically, CAP1 knockdown suppressed neuroinflammation via the Cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate (cAMP)/ Protein Kinase A (PKA)/Nuclear Factor kappa‑light‑chain‑enhancer of activated B cells (NF‑κB) pathway, as shown by reduced p‑PKA/p‑P65, cAMP, and pro‑inflammatory cytokines (Interleukin‑6, IL‑6; Interleukin‑1 beta, IL‑1β; Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha, TNF‑α). Consistent with this, an NF‑κB agonist completely blocked the anxiolytic effects of CAP1 knockdown, confirming that CAP1 acts through this signaling cascade to promote cytokine release and subsequent synaptic remodeling. Collectively, these findings establish ACC CAP1 as a critical mediator of chronic pain‑induced anxiety in male mice and suggest that targeting CAP1 may represent a promising strategy for precision intervention in pain-related affective disorders.

title: Ventral striatal and caudate contributions to episodic retrieval.
abstract: Striatal activity during episodic memory retrieval is a robust phenomenon observed across various stimulus types and experimental paradigms. Previous research suggests that the ventral striatum and the caudate contribute differentially to retrieval processes: ventral striatal activity is posited to vary with the intrinsic reward of successful retrieval, whereas caudate activity is attributed to effortful cognitive control. The present fMRI study aimed to test the overarching hypothesis that these striatal subregions make distinct contributions to episodic retrieval and to further specify their functional roles. To this end, we employed a word-picture paired-associates learning paradigm in which words served as cues in two consecutive cued-recall tests that were separated by 24 hrs. Participants indicated the specificity of their associative memories, enabling characterization of striatal response profiles as a function of associative memory specificity and treatment of memory specificity as a proxy for the intrinsic reward associated with retrieval success. Rather than being not readily compatible with a role of the caudate in effortful post-retrieval control, the results suggest that elevated caudate activity during successful recall reflects pre-retrieval control or involuntary orienting to salient mnemonic information. In contrast, rather than reflect intrinsic reward itself, ventral striatal activity varied with the discrepancy between expected and actual intrinsic reward elicited by retrieval outcomes-that is, a metacognitive reward prediction error. Moreover, ventral striatum signaled the relevance of retrieved information and modulated its re-encoding to facilitate future retrievals.

title: The effect of concurrent application of the deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens and cannabidiol injection during extinction period on reinstatement of METH-induced conditioned place preference in extinguished rats.
abstract: Methamphetamine (METH) is a potent stimulant drug that significantly alters the function of the central nervous system (CNS). METHS's abuse may be linked with a variety of psychiatric disorders, primarily by affecting the reward system. Cannabidiol (CBD), a primary cannabinoid component of the Cannabis plant, has been shown to affect the reward system, suggesting it for modulating addictive behaviors. On the other hand, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the nucleus accumbens (NAc), one of the most significant brain regions implicated in mediating rewards, is effective in alleviating drug-seeking behaviors. The present research aimed to evaluate the effects of low-frequency DBS, CBD, and a combination of both on the extinction and reinstatement of METH-induced conditioned place preference (CPP). CBD was injected into the lateral ventricle at doses of 2.5, 5, and 10 μg/5 μL, and low-frequency DBS (10 Hz, for 30 minutes) was administered to the NAc, both during the extinction phase. The results showed CBD (10 µg/5 µL) or DBS facilitated extinction. DBS decreased mean extinction latency but did not differ significantly from CBD (10 µg/5 µL) alone. The combination groups at all tested CBD doses showed reduced mean extinction latency compared with the control groups; only the 10 µg/5 µL combination group differed significantly from DBS alone. However, neither CBD (10 µg/5 µL) alone nor DBS altered the CPP score on the reinstatement day. Combination of DBS and CBD administration (at all doses) significantly decreased the CPP score on the reinstatement day. In conclusion, it can be suggested that CBD may be beneficial for alleviating METH-induced reinstatement in combination with DBS, while both alone had no effect.

title: Convergent Microglial and Astrocytic Responses across Diverse Stress Paradigms: Integrating Inflammation, Metabolism, and Behavior.
abstract: The central nervous system responds to diverse challenges through convergent glial mechanisms, yet most reviews examine single stressor paradigms in isolation. This review uniquely integrates current knowledge across five major stress categories (psychosocial, immune/inflammatory, infectious, injury/damage, and metabolic), revealing both shared pathways and stimulus-specific glial responses that have not been systematically compared. Because microglia and astrocytes are the principal immune-metabolic sensors mediating these responses, this review is centered on these two cell types, while acknowledging that oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and ependymal cells also participate in stress-related glial pathology, particularly with respect to white matter and cerebrospinal fluid homeostasis. While all stressors activate common inflammatory cascades including NF-κB signaling, complement activation, and inflammasome assembly, they elicit distinguishable molecular signatures. For instance, psychosocial stress uniquely engages type I interferon responses driving microglial synapse elimination. Viral infections produce severe metabolic reprogramming, hijacking host metabolism to support viral replication while depleting cellular NAD+ and ATP. Autoimmune inflammation generates lipid-laden disease-associated microglia with upregulated cholesterol metabolism genes. Unlike previous reviews focusing solely on inflammation or metabolism, we emphasize their bidirectional integration as a unifying principle. Inflammatory signals trigger metabolic shifts toward aerobic glycolysis, generating lactate serving dual functions as neuronal fuel and inflammatory mediator. This metabolic reprogramming, orchestrated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, and mTOR, creates feedback loops linking glial dysfunction to neuronal alterations. Complement-mediated synaptic pruning, disrupted neuron-glia metabolic coupling, and impaired neurotrophic support converge to produce depression, cognitive impairment, and sickness behaviors. Individual variability reflects interactions among genetic factors, sex, age, and blood-brain barrier integrity. This cross-paradigm comparative approach identifies high-value therapeutic targets applicable across multiple conditions rather than single diseases. We propose integrated intervention strategies simultaneously targeting inflammatory and metabolic pathways, guided by single-cell profiling for personalized medicine tailored to individual patient molecular signatures. We further discuss the conceptual overlaps inherent to the five-category classification scheme adopted here and outline the limitations of extrapolating across heterogeneous stress paradigms, glial cell types, and species.

title: Heart-brain co-ageing: phenotypic heterogeneity, molecular mechanisms and translational interventions.
abstract: Population ageing has increased the burden of cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline and frailty in older adults. These conditions are often studied separately, yet increasing evidence suggests that the ageing heart, vasculature and brain are biologically interconnected. Using a hybrid design that combines a systematic literature search with narrative synthesis, this review summarizes current knowledge on heart-brain co-ageing, with emphasis on phenotypic heterogeneity, molecular mechanisms and translational interventions. Heart-brain co-ageing is characterized by partially coupled but non-synchronous ageing trajectories of cardiac, vascular and brain function. Major clinical phenotypes include vascular-dominant ageing, cardiac-output-related brain vulnerability, arrhythmia-associated thromboinflammatory injury, frailty-cognitive decline and metabolic-inflammatory co-ageing. These phenotypes differ in risk profiles, dominant mechanisms and potential biomarkers. Candidate shared mechanisms include cellular senescence, chronic low-grade inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, endothelial impairment, blood-brain barrier disruption, epigenetic remodelling, telomere attrition, non-coding ribonucleic acid regulation, Klotho signalling, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide metabolism and microbiome-derived metabolic signalling. Advances in multimodal imaging, circulating biomarkers, biological ageing clocks and multi-omics profiling provide new opportunities for risk stratification, although clinical standardization remains limited. Heart-brain co-ageing should not be regarded as the simple coexistence of cardiovascular and neurological diseases, but as a dynamic multi-organ ageing process shaped by shared biological drivers, interorgan interactions and organ-specific vulnerability, and we propose it as a testable conceptual framework with explicit operational criteria that distinguish coupled from parallel organ ageing. Future research should integrate longitudinal phenotyping, mechanism-based biomarkers and stratified clinical trials to develop precision interventions that preserve both cardiovascular and brain health in older adults.

title: The neuropathy-causing GARS1∆ETAQ mutation drives pathology in subsets of motor and sensory neurons in mice.
abstract: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2D (CMT2D) results from gain-of-function mutations in GARS1, which encodes glycyl-tRNA synthetase (GlyRS), the enzyme responsible for charging transfer RNA (tRNA) with glycine. There are several CMT2D mouse models, but Gars∆ETAQ/+ is the only one that bears a patient-sourced mutation. Created using CRISPR/Cas9 to model a 12-nucleotide de novo GARS1 deletion identified in an unusually severe CMT2D patient, Gars∆ETAQ/+ mice have previously been shown to display several neuromuscular phenotypes: motor axon loss, denervated neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) and reduced muscle function. Here, we extend these analyses to provide a more comprehensive understanding of both motor and sensory nerve deficits across hind- and fore-limbs. At 3 months, Gars∆ETAQ/+ mice possess sex-independent alterations in the levels of neuropathy biomarkers - including decreased NfL and increased periaxin - alongside reduced muscle endurance and strength, and impairments in the sensory modalities of mechanosensation, proprioception and nociception. Underpinning these dysfunctions, we identified site-specific defects comprising altered sensory neuron populations, muscle spindle loss, reduced motor neuron size, disrupted NMJ innervation and maturation, and reduced axonal transport of signalling endosomes in vivo. Together, these experiments show that Gars∆ETAQ/+ mice display robust and selective peripheral nerve pathology that manifests in a general length-dependent fashion, priming this CMT2D allele for testing treatments and evaluating mechanisms underlying peripheral nerve vulnerability.

title: The Basal Ganglia Talk Back: Striato-Cortical and Pallido-Cortical Return Pathways in Basal Ganglia-Cortical Communication.
abstract: A central framework in basal ganglia neuroscience is that the cerebral cortex sends excitatory information to the striatum, where it is integrated with thalamic and neuromodulatory signals to shape action selection, learning, and behavioral flexibility [1-10]. In this classical view, the striatum acts as the major input structure of the basal ganglia, whereas processed output returns to the cortex indirectly through pallidal, nigral, and thalamocortical pathways [1-4, 10, 11]. However, recent evidence indicates that striatal and pallidal circuits can influence cortical processing through more direct, specialized, and neurochemically diverse routes than previously appreciated [12-16], revealing an unexpected diversity of basal ganglia return pathways. In particular, the identification of a previously uncharacterized cholinergic projection from the dorsal tail of the striatum to the auditory cortex suggests that specialized striatal circuits can directly modulate cortical sensory processing [15]. These findings provide a new entry point for reconsidering basal ganglia-cortical communication beyond the classical indirect loop model. In this review, we use this striato-cortical cholinergic pathway as a recent example, considered alongside the more established pallidocortical literature, to discuss the emerging concept of striato-pallidal-cortical return signaling. We first revisit the historical organization of corticostriatal and basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops, discuss the dorsal tail of the striatum as a sensory-associated basal ganglia node, and finally integrate recent evidence for direct and reciprocal pallidocortical pathways. Together, we propose an expanded model in which basal ganglia circuits may influence cortical gain, timing, sensory salience, and behavioral relevance through multiple return channels. Rather than replacing the classical model, this emerging view expands it: the striatum is not only a recipient of cortical input, but also a participant in return pathways that can contribute to shaping cortical computation.

title: Loss of APOBEC1 disrupts RNA editing homeostasis and accelerates prion disease progression.
abstract: RNA editing is an epitranscriptomic mechanism that shapes transcriptome diversity and fine-tunes neuronal function. While adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing by ADAR enzymes has been extensively studied in neurodegenerative disorders, the role of cytidine-to-uridine (C-to-U) editing catalyzed by APOBEC1 remains largely unexplored. We investigated the impact of APOBEC1 on RNA editing homeostasis and prion disease progression using complementary in vitro and in vivo models. Global RNA editing and gene expression profiles were established in non-infected N2A and prion-infected sc-N2A murine neuroblastoma cells, under control conditions or following APOBEC1 depletion. APOBEC1 was silenced by shRNA-mediated knockdown to assess its regulatory contribution. In vivo disease progression was assessed in Apobec1 knockout mice subjected to RML prion infection to evaluate survival outcomes. Prion infection was associated with a global increase in RNA editing and an expanded repertoire of edited transcripts in sc-N2A cells. APOBEC1 depletion markedly reduced the overall editing levels, affecting both A-to-I and C-to-U editing events, reshaping editing patterns in transcripts associated with RNA and protein transport, cellular stress responses, synaptic signaling, and neuroimmune interactions. Consistently, Apobec1 KO mice exhibited accelerated body weight loss and significantly shortened survival following RML prion challenge. These findings support APOBEC1 as a contributor to RNA editing homeostasis and suggest that APOBEC1 loss reduces resilience to prion-induced neurodegenerative stress. APOBEC1 deficiency was associated with altered editome profiles in prion-infected cells and accelerated disease progression in the RML prion model.

title: Epivascular Glia and Macular Pigment Changes after Faricimab or Aflibercept during the Loading Phase in Diabetic Macular Edema: A Prospective Non-randomized Pilot Study.
abstract: To explore short-term changes in epivascular glia (EVG), macular pigment optical density (MPOD), visual acuity, and retinal thickness after faricimab or aflibercept in treatment-naive eyes with center-involving diabetic macular edema (DME). This prospective, non-randomized pilot study included 30 eyes with DME and EVG on en face optical coherence tomography. Fifteen eyes received three monthly injections of faricimab 6 mg and 15 received aflibercept 2 mg. The primary exploratory outcome was complete EVG regression after loading. Secondary outcomes included best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), central macular thickness (CMT), MPOD, fluid resolution, and resolution of traction-related abnormalities. Complete EVG regression occurred in 12/15 eyes (80.0%) with faricimab and 6/15 (40.0%) with aflibercept (Fisher's exact p=0.060). Resolution of traction- related abnormalities occurred in 11/15 (73.3%) and 5/15 eyes (33.3%), respectively (p=0.066). Post-loading CMT was 274.5 ± 61.3 versus 328.7 ± 72.4 µm (unadjusted p=0.035), MPOD was 0.46 ± 0.07 versus 0.39 ± 0.08 (unadjusted p=0.017), and BCVA was 0.27 ± 0.14 versus 0.36 ± 0.16 logMAR (p=0.112). EVG and traction- related outcomes were numerically more favorable with faricimab but were not statistically significant. Exploratory anatomical and MPOD differences require confirmation in larger randomized studies.

title: COMPREHENSIVE ORAL CARE IS ASSOCIATED WITH A SIGNIFICANT DECREASE IN VENTILATOR-ASSOCIATED PNEUMONIA: A SINGLE CENTER PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY.
abstract: Mechanically ventilated patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are at risk for developing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), with a 13% mortality rate and cost of $50,000 per patient. Toothbrushing is associated with positive outcomes, including lower VAP rates. Electric toothbrushes (eTBs) have greater effectiveness in the general population compared with manual toothbrushes (mTBs), and eTBs may provide benefits to ventilated patients. The aim of the study was to evaluate VAP rates for patients receiving a comprehensive oral care protocol (COCP) including an eTB versus a standard oral care protocol (SOCP) including an mTB. We conducted a prospective cohort study in a tertiary hospital's ICUs. SOCP or COCP consisting of an electric toothbrush was followed. VAP rates and hospital costs were compared between groups. Our study included 72 ICU patients (63.9% male, mean age 53.5±16.6 years). Patients treated with COCP were less likely to develop VAP (2.6% vs 21.2%, P=0.020), had significantly fewer ventilation days (5.4±1.8 vs 6.2±1.3, P=0.031), and fewer ICU days (9.0±5.6 vs 13.8±9.1, P=0.012). The COCP group had significantly fewer VAPs per 1,000 patient ventilation days, 1 in 209 days, or 4.8 (0.1-26.7) events per 1,000 ventilation days versus standard oral care with 7 in 190 days or 36.8 (14.8-75.9), P=0.037. Cost savings if COCP would have been used in the SOCP group of 33 patients were estimated at $283,428. We compared standard versus comprehensive oral care protocols. Significantly fewer patients treated with the comprehensive protocol developed VAP and hospital savings were significant.

title: Lipid dysregulation in polyglutamine diseases.
abstract: Polyglutamine (polyQ) diseases are fatal neurodegenerative disorders caused by pathological CAG repeat expansions in disease-associated genes. They are characterized by progressive motor dysfunction and typically late onset. Although multiple mechanisms have been proposed, accumulating evidence indicates that lipid dysregulation contributes to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Lipids are essential for brain development and homeostasis, and disrupted lipid metabolism is implicated across neurodegenerative conditions. Within the polyQ spectrum, Huntington's disease is the best studied and shows strong links between altered lipid pathways and neuronal pathology, whereas the role of lipid dysregulation in other polyQ disorders remains less well defined. In this review, we summarize key lipid functions in the central nervous system, synthesize reported lipid alterations across polyQ diseases, and evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting lipid metabolism.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Plant Secondary Metabolites in Modulation of ROS-mediated Microglial Activation and Neuroinflammation: Special Emphasize to Quercetin.
abstract: Neuroinflammation is a central pathogenic mechanism in numerous neurological disorders, with microglia playing a pivotal role in coordinating immune responses through tightly regulated redox, metabolic, and inflammatory signaling pathways. While transient microglial activation supports tissue homeostasis and repair, persistent activation promotes excessive production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS), pro-inflammatory mediators, and lipid-derived inflammatory signals, driving chronic neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. Accordingly, modulation of microglial activation has emerged as an attractive therapeutic strategy. Plant-derived extracts and phytochemicals represent a remarkable source of bioactive molecules such as quercetin, which are able to concomitantly modulate multiple pathways involved in microglial activation. Over the past two decades, numerous studies have investigated their effects using immortalized murine BV-2 cells and, to a lesser extent, primary microglia. Despite differences between these experimental models, current evidence reveals a striking convergence of molecular mechanisms. Plant-derived metabolites consistently attenuate microglial activation through inhibition of the NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways, activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant axis, suppression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), and pro-inflammatory cytokine production, while limiting oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. Emerging evidence further indicates that these compounds regulate microglial phenotypic plasticity, mitochondrial function, immunometabolic reprogramming, and, potentially, peroxisomal metabolism and mitochondria-peroxisome crosstalk, thereby extending their actions well beyond conventional antioxidant activity. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms by which plant-derived extracts and phytochemicals regulate microglial function, with particular emphasis on the interconnected networks linking redox homeostasis, inflammatory signaling, lipid metabolism, and organelle communication.

title: Activating systemic inflammation with lipopolysaccharide drives microglia-mediated degradation of perineuronal nets after cervical spinal cord injury in female rats.
abstract: Functional gains from rehabilitative motor training after spinal cord injury (SCI) depend on neuroplasticity, which naturally declines over time. We previously demonstrated that combining the pro-inflammatory compound lipopolysaccharide (LPS) with motor training reawakens neuroplasticity and enhances its therapeutic efficacy in chronic cervical SCI rats, though the underlying mechanisms remained unclear. Here, we investigated whether LPS-induced inflammation facilitates neuroplasticity by degrading perineuronal nets (PNNs), extracellular structures known to restrict recovery after SCI. Adult female Lewis rats received a single intraperitoneal LPS injection (1.5 mg/kg) ten days post-cervical SCI. In the first experiment, five days post-injection, we observed significantly diminished PNN marker fluorescence around ventral horn motor neurons in spared, injury-reactive spinal cord regions. To determine the cellular mechanism, we conducted a second experiment in which we pharmacologically attenuated microglial activity using minocycline (35 mg/kg). Minocycline treatment successfully prevented the LPS-induced loss of PNN fluorescence, demonstrating that microglia actively mediate PNN breakdown. Collectively, these findings provide a proof-of-concept mechanism by which inflammation influences neuroplasticity following central nervous system injury. Our observations support the growing recognition that inflammation, far from being exclusively detrimental, holds the capacity to contribute to healing after injury. By activating microglia to degrade PNNs, LPS-induced inflammation removes the structural barrier surrounding motor neurons, potentially priming them to be more responsive to the neuroplastic changes induced by rehabilitative motor training, providing a plausible explanation for our previously reported outcomes. This study highlights neuroimmune interactions as key regulators of neuroplasticity and the therapeutic efficacy of rehabilitative interventions in neurological disorders.

title: Intravenous administration of a PHP.eB vector overexpressing neuronal Caveolin-1 delays motor neuron and neuromuscular degeneration in a TDP-43 mouse model of ALS.
abstract: TDP-43 proteinopathy is observed in over 95% of ALS cases, yet effective disease-modifying therapies remain elusive. We previously showed that neuron-specific overexpression of caveolin-1 via SynCav1 extended survival and delayed neurodegeneration in an SOD1 mouse model of ALS. Here, we further assessed the effect of systemic delivery of AAV-PHP.eB-SynCav1 in TDP-43A315T mice. At 24 weeks, SynCav1-treated mice showed preserved motor neuron (MN) morphology, maintained neuromuscular junction (NMJ) innervation, and normalized pathologically driven neurotrophic transcription in the spinal cord. Immunoblotting revealed that SynCav1 increased calcium-impermeable GluA2 in membrane lipid rafts of lumbar SC. However, these effects diminished with disease progression: by 32 weeks, lumbar MN loss and NMJ denervation were no longer significantly different between TDP-43-SynNull and TDP-43-SynCav1 mice, although partial protection was observed in the cervical spinal cord. These findings establish SynCav1 as an effective early-phase neuroprotective strategy and highlight the need for combinatorial approaches to achieve sustained protection.

title: Safety and efficacy of delpacibart zotadirsen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy mutations amenable to exon 44 skipping in the USA (EXPLORE44): a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, phase 1/2 trial.
abstract: There are no approved exon skipping therapies to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy due to DMD variants amenable to exon 44 skipping (DMD44). Delpacibart zotadirsen (del-zota, also known as AOC 1044) is a first-in-class antibody-oligonucleotide conjugate designed to deliver an exon 44-skipping phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer to muscle to restore dystrophin expression for individuals with DMD44. EXPLORE44 was a first-in-human trial to evaluate del-zota's safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and efficacy. EXPLORE44 was a two-part randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 1/2 study in healthy adult men (aged 18-55 years; part A) and ambulatory and non-ambulatory male participants with DMD44 (aged 7-27 years; part B) at ten clinical research sites in the USA. Dosing in part B was informed by safety, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic data from part A. In part B, participants with DMD44 were randomised (3:1 del-zota:placebo) within two dose cohorts to receive three intravenous doses of del-zota (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks, or 10 mg/kg every 8 weeks) or matching placebo. A computer-generated permuted-block randomisation schedule was prepared by an independent statistician with no further role in the study. Infusions were prepared by an unmasked pharmacist under supervision of the masked investigator; other site staff, participants, and sponsor team members were masked to allocation. The primary objective was safety and tolerability measured by the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events. Secondary endpoints assessing target engagement were change from baseline in exon skipping (ie, defined as the percentage of dystrophin mRNA transcripts in which exon 44 is excluded from the mature mRNA relative to total dystrophin mRNA transcripts) and dystrophin level to month 4 (5 mg/kg cohort) or month 5 (10 mg/kg cohort). The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05670730) and is complete. Between Dec 5, 2022, and June 27, 2024, we enrolled and randomly assigned 45 healthy volunteers and 26 men and boys with DMD44. In part A, three (30%) of ten healthy volunteers who received placebo and 21 (62%) of 34 who received del-zota reported at least one adverse event, none of which were severe or serious. In part B, nine participants with DMD44 received del-zota at 5 mg/kg, ten at 10 mg/kg, and seven received placebo; mean age 13·3 years (SD 4·2). 16 (84%) participants with DMD44 treated with del-zota and six (86%) treated with placebo reported at least one adverse event, most of which were mild or moderate; two participants, both in the 5 mg/kg del-zota group, discontinued due to adverse events (anaphylactic reaction and infusion-related reaction). Mean increases from baseline in exon 44 skipping were 36·6% (95% CI 20·8 to 52·4, SD 17·1, nominal p=0·0013) at 5 mg/kg, 43·4% (32·8 to 54·0, 14·9, nominal p<0·0001) at 10 mg/kg, and 1·6% (-3·4 to 6·7, 4·8, nominal p=0·44) with placebo. Mean increases from baseline in dystrophin levels were 25·0% (9·2 to 40·7, 17·0, nominal p=0·0082) at 5 mg/kg, 25·6% (13·0 to 38·3, 17·7, nominal p=0·0013) at 10 mg/kg, and -0·7% (-4·8 to 3·3, 3·9, nominal p=0·66) with placebo. Del-zota had an acceptable safety profile, produced increases in exon 44 skipping and dystrophin expression, and decreased biomarkers of muscle damage in participants with DMD44. Findings from this study support further investigation of del-zota in a phase 3 study to assess efficacy and long-term safety. Avidity Biosciences, A Novartis Company.

title: Staged bilateral focused ultrasound pallidothalamic tractotomy for Parkinson's disease - Authors' reply.
Staged bilateral focused ultrasound pallidothalamic tractotomy for Parkinson's disease.
Reframing traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury as chronic multisystem disorders: toward integrated, long-term care.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) affect more than 220 million people worldwide and are associated with cardiometabolic, endocrine, neurological, and psychiatric sequelae for years to decades after an acute injury. However, most health systems still treat neurotrauma (TBI and SCI, collectively) as a time-limited event, leaving long-term surveillance of these patients fragmented or absent, which leads to preventable mortality and avoidable readmissions. TBI and SCI in adults should be reclassified as acute-onset multisystem chronic-risk conditions. Existing cardiovascular, endocrine, and psychiatric services do not capture neurotrauma-specific risks, including trauma-induced hypopituitarism, autonomic dysregulation, accelerated ageing, and cognitive-behavioural impairment, so neurotrauma care is best framed as a missing node in chronic neurological care. We propose a risk-stratified pathway of care navigation, multisystem screening, and telehealth; convergence with adjacent stroke, cardiometabolic, memory, psychiatric, pain, and epilepsy services; and the financing, workforce, and registry reforms needed to deliver measurable reductions in 5-year mortality, avoidable rehospitalisation, and long-term disability.

title: Change in HbA1c and weight after initiation of antipsychotic treatment in people with severe mental illness in England: an individual-level interrupted time-series analysis.
abstract: Second-generation antipsychotics contribute to excess cardiometabolic morbidity in people with severe mental illness, but the timing of early glycaemic change and whether it parallels weight gain remain unclear. We aimed to evaluate glycated haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) and weight trajectories before and after initiation of antipsychotic treatment. We conducted an individual-level interrupted time-series analysis in England using electronic health records (EHR) from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum database between Jan 1, 2000, and June 7, 2023. Included participants were aged 18-59 years with severe mental illness (SMI) who had at least a second oral second-generation antipsychotic prescription issued within 90 days from their first antipsychotic prescription. Individuals were excluded if they had dementia, type 2 diabetes, or antipsychotic prescriptions before age 18 years. The exposure was the first recorded oral initiation of antipsychotic treatment. We used individual-level, interrupted time-series mixed models with linear splines to estimate rates of change in HbA1c and weight in people with SMI before treatment initiation, 0-90 days after initiation, and from 91 days to 2 years after initiation. An additional outcome was time to type 2 diabetes diagnosis or antidiabetic medication prescription. Analyses were stratified by sex, antipsychotic drug, and baseline glycaemic status. People with lived experience contributed to the research question, study approach, interpretation, and dissemination. Of the 96 849 eligible individuals, 53 558 (55·3%) were male and 43 291 (44·7%) were female. The mean age of participants was 37·2 years (SD 11·1; range 18-59); 62 683 (64·7%) reported their ethnicity as White, 5952 (6·1%) as south Asian, 6736 (7·0%) as Black, 3793 (3·9%) as other or mixed ethnicity, and 17 693 (18·3%) had missing ethnicity. 74 233 (76·6%) individuals had at least one recorded weight measurement and 24 084 (24·9%) had at least one HbA1c measurement. In the pre-treatment period, HbA1c increased at a rate of 0·01 mmol/mol per week (95% CI 0·00-0·01) and weight at a rate of 0·02 kg (0·02-0·02) per week. In the 0-90 days following antipsychotic treatment initiation, HbA1c increased at a rate of 0·12 mmol/mol per week (0·09-0·15) and weight at 0·21 kg (0·20-0·22) per week. From day 91 to 2 years, the rate of increase of HbA1c returned to pre-treatment levels (0·01 mmol/mol per week [0·00-0·01]) and weight increased at 0·03 kg (0·02-0·03) per week. Increases were largest for olanzapine (HbA1c 0·18 mmol/mol per week [95% CI 0·12-0·25]; weight 0·28 kg [0·27-0·30]) and generally higher among women (HbA1c 0·14 mmol/mol [0·09-0·18]; weight 0·22 kg [0·21-0·23]).
